title: Fal raises $1.3B at a $16B valuation, led by Bessemer
description:
AI infrastructure company fal has closed a $1.3 billion Series F round, as reported by Tech.eu. Bessemer Venture Partners led the round, with NVIDIA, Sound Ventures, HOF Capital and T. Rowe Price also taking part.

The numbers

Fal announced the Series F together with a $350 million Series E that Sequoia Capital led in April. The two rounds add up to $1.65 billion. Citing Bloomberg, Tech.eu says the new round values the company at $16 billion, twice the $8 billion valuation from April. Fal was founded in 2021 by Burkay Gür and Görkem Yurtseven.

What fal does

The company builds infrastructure for generative media. Businesses use it to run image, video and audio models at scale and to fit generative AI into the production and creative workflows they already have. The source names entertainment, advertising, e-commerce, gaming and marketing as the main customer industries.

During 2026, fal has worked on the quality and speed of generative media models using post-training techniques. It also continues to develop its own models next to those supplied by partners.

Where the money goes

According to the source, the funding will pay for expanding fal's inference infrastructure and team, and for further work on its generative media technology. The company plans to put money into research and test new approaches to AI-assisted content creation through 2027.

What the source does not say

The article gives no new product, model, price or plan, and no customer terms. Any effect on the cost or speed of generating media for fal's users is not stated and remains unconfirmed.

Why it is on our radar

Generative media is moving from experiments to a layer that companies build production work on, and the investor list in this round points to continued capital for the compute underneath it. For a business that buys such capacity through an API, the practical questions concern vendor dependence and portability rather than the valuation itself.

title: Meta buys Conductor; its cloud service closes November 20
description:
Meta has acquired Conductor, an AI coding startup, according to TechCrunch, which says Axios reported the news first. Meta confirmed the deal to TechCrunch but declined to share further details, so price and terms are unknown.

What Conductor does

Conductor lets a software engineer start a project by putting several agents to work in separate, parallel workspaces, each handling its own part of the job. The agent teams can run in the cloud, on a local machine, or through a phone. The agents are not Conductor's own; they come from major labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI. The company was founded in 2024 and shipped its core product only last summer.

What changes for current users

Founder and CEO Charlie Holtz announced that Conductor is joining Meta. He said the core features will keep working as they do today until early next year, and that the team plans "something new" for customers by then. What that product will be has not been described, so treat it as unconfirmed.

The exception is the cloud service. It shuts down on November 20, and Conductor will then start deleting user cloud data. Anyone with work stored there has a short window to move it.

Why Meta wants it

TechCrunch describes Meta as a company that has spent recent months catching up in AI services. In August it launched its own coding agent, Muse Code. Meta also reported that its Muse agents have passed 10 million users. The Conductor deal adds to a run of AI acquisitions over the past year, including the agent platform Moltbook.

Holtz said he is looking forward to working with Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, and Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta's Superintelligence Labs.

What to watch

The source does not say whether Conductor will keep supporting agents from Anthropic and OpenAI after the move to Meta, or whether the next product will be tied to Meta's own models. Until Meta says so, plan on the assumption that today's setup is temporary.

title: Human-in-the-loop architecture
description:
Human‑in‑the‑Loop Architecture Primer

A repeatable, auditable workflow turns a proposal into an execution only after a deterministic series of checks. By binding the human‑approval token to the exact payload, the decision becomes a verifiable part of the transaction rather than a post‑hoc disclaimer.

The architecture distinguishes four sources of truth:

  • Current knowledge – stored in the context or retrieval component.
  • Live values – obtained from authoritative APIs at request time.
  • Enforceable business rules – expressed as deterministic code that must be satisfied before any state change.
  • Model tuning – performed after systematic evaluation and labeling; it supplements but does not replace rule‑based enforcement or freshness checks.

Quick‑Diagnosis Table

Symptom Likely Root Cause Immediate Mitigation
Unauthorized data mutation after automation Approval not cryptographically tied to payload Introduce payload hash in the approval token
Escalating reviewer backlog on high‑risk actions Flat approval process regardless of impact Tier risk and assign reviewer capacity
Irreversible financial adjustments cannot be rolled back Execution step runs before final sign‑off Enforce exact‑action approval as the last gate
Audit logs missing key fields Logging tied to mutable objects Serialize immutable request snapshots

Decision Flow 

flowchart TD
    A["Proposal"] --> B["Risk‑Policy Evaluation"]
    B --> C["Tier Assignment"]
    C --> D["Exact‑Action Approval"]
    D --> E["Execution"]
    E --> F["Immutable Audit Record"]

The flow consists of Proposal → Risk‑Policy → Exact‑Action Approval → Execution. The final audit record captures the hash‑bound token, tier, reviewer identifiers and timestamps.

Architecture Responsibilities

Component Primary Responsibility Guarantees (intent)
Proposal Engine Emit a JSON payload describing the intended mutation; compute a deterministic SHA‑256 hash Payload immutability (via hash)
Risk‑Policy Service Apply deterministic rules, assign a risk tier, and expose a risk score Consistent tier assignment
Approval Service Present the exact payload + hash to a reviewer; on sign‑off, issue a signed token containing the hash Human decision binding
Execution Engine Verify token signature and payload hash before invoking downstream actions Tamper‑evidence
Audit Logger Persist an immutable event (e.g., append‑only log) with full payload, hash and approval token Non‑repudiation

Python Helper – Decision & Payload Binding 

# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
"""
Teaching‑only helper that demonstrates:
1. deterministic risk tiering,
2. creation of a hash‑bound approval token,
3. verification before execution.

All dependencies are from the Python standard library.
"""

import json
import hashlib
import hmac
import time
from typing import Dict, Literal, TypedDict

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Types
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
class Payload(TypedDict):
    action: str                     # e.g. "adjust_credit_limit"
    entity_id: str                  # unique identifier of the subject
    parameters: Dict[str, float]  # e.g. {"value_change": 25000.0}
    requested_by: str               # service or user ID

RiskTier = Literal[1, 2, 3]

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Deterministic risk policy
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
def risk_tier(payload: Payload) -> RiskTier:
    """
    Simple deterministic rule set.
    - Tier 1: value_change < 1 000 and reversible
    - Tier 2: value_change < 10 000 and reversible
    - Tier 3: otherwise (potentially irreversible)
    """
    change = payload["parameters"].get("value_change", 0.0)
    irreversible = payload["parameters"].get("irreversible", False)

    if change < 1_000 and not irreversible:
        return 1
    if change < 10_000 and not irreversible:
        return 2
    return 3

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Payload hashing
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
def payload_hash(payload: Payload) -> str:
    """
    Returns a hex‑encoded SHA‑256 over the canonical JSON representation.
    """
    canonical = json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
    return hashlib.sha256(canonical.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Token creation (illustrative only)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
SECRET_KEY = b"super‑secret‑key‑rotate‑daily"

def create_approval_token(payload: Payload, reviewer: str) -> str:
    """
    Very simple JWT‑like token: header.body.signature.
    Intended for teaching – a production system should use a robust JWT library.
    """
    header = json.dumps({"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT"}).encode()
    body = json.dumps(
        {
            "sub": reviewer,
            "iat": int(time.time()),
            "hash": payload_hash(payload),
        }
    ).encode()
    signature = hmac.new(SECRET_KEY, header + b"." + body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    token = f"{header.hex()}.{body.hex()}.{signature}"
    return token

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Verification before execution
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
def verify_and_execute(payload: Payload, token: str) -> None:
    """
    Confirms that the token’s hash matches the supplied payload.
    Raises AssertionError on mismatch – in a real system this would abort the transaction.
    """
    header_hex, body_hex, signature = token.split(".")
    body = json.loads(bytes.fromhex(body_hex))
    expected_hash = payload_hash(payload)

    assert body["hash"] == expected_hash, "Payload hash mismatch – possible tampering"
    expected_sig = hmac.new(
        SECRET_KEY, f"{header_hex}.{body_hex}".encode(), hashlib.sha256
    ).hexdigest()
    assert signature == expected_sig, "Invalid approval signature"

    # ----- Execution placeholder -----
    print(f"Executing {payload['action']} for {payload['entity_id']} …")
    # Replace with an idempotent, atomic operation in production.

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Example usage (not executed in docs)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    example: Payload = {
        "action": "adjust_credit_limit",
        "entity_id": "cust-12345",
        "parameters": {"value_change": 2_500.0, "irreversible": False},
        "requested_by": "loan‑engine",
    }

    tier = risk_tier(example)
    assert tier == 2, "Tier assignment mismatch in example"

    token = create_approval_token(example, reviewer="compliance‑officer")
    verify_and_execute(example, token)

Teaching‑Only – The code uses only the standard library and a fixed secret key for clarity. Replace the token logic with a production‑grade JWT implementation and rotate secrets regularly.

Architectural Decision Records (ADRs)

ADR 001 – Payload‑Hash Binding

Context

Early prototypes stored the human sign‑off flag in a mutable column. Audits later revealed that downstream services could modify the underlying request after approval, weakening accountability.

Decision

Include a cryptographic hash of the exact payload in the approval token. Execution components must verify the hash before performing any state change.

Implications

  • Positive – Provides evidence that the approved payload has not been altered. Auditors can recompute the hash from immutable logs.
  • Negative – Legitimate changes (e.g., enrichment) require a new approval round, which may increase latency for low‑risk items.

Acceptance Criteria

  1. Audit logs contain both the payload hash and the approval token.
  2. Unit tests confirm that modifying a payload after token issuance raises an AssertionError.

ADR 002 – Tier‑Based Reviewer Load Balancing

Context

A single compliance team was overloaded by a mix of low‑ and high‑risk proposals, causing SLA pressures for high‑impact actions.

Decision

Define three deterministic risk tiers with distinct reviewer requirements:

Tier Max Δ Value Irreversibility Reviewers Required
1 < 1 000 No 0 (auto‑approve after sanity check)
2 < 10 000 No 1 (single reviewer)
3 ≥ 10 000 Yes 2 (dual sign‑off)

Tier 1 proposals are routed to an automated sanity check; Tier 3 actions trigger a dedicated dual‑approval queue.

Implications

  • Positive – Reviewer effort aligns with risk, reducing backlog for high‑impact changes.
  • Negative – The tiering function must remain deterministic; any change to the rule set requires a versioned policy rollout.

Acceptance Criteria

  1. Simulated runs confirm that identical payloads are consistently assigned the same tier across service versions.
  2. Policy version is recorded with each decision; a mismatch between recorded and expected version causes the decision to be rejected.

Evaluation & Maintenance Checklist

  • [ ] Deterministic Policy – Verify that the risk‑policy service returns the same tier for identical payloads across successive runs.
  • [ ] Hash Integrity – Run a periodic job that recomputes payload hashes from audit logs and compares them to stored token hashes.
  • [ ] Signature Rotation – Rotate the signing secret on a defined schedule; ensure services accept both current and previous keys during overlap.
  • [ ] Reviewer Load Monitoring – Track average queue time per tier; adjust staffing or automation when thresholds are exceeded.
  • [ ] Irreversibility Guardrail – For Tier 3 actions, require an explicit “I understand this is irreversible” acknowledgment, logged as a separate event.
  • [ ] Regulatory Change Process – When new regulations appear, update the risk‑policy rule set, increment the policy version, and back‑test against historic proposals before production rollout.
  • [ ] Test Coverage – Include unit tests for risk_tier, payload_hash, and token verification; add integration tests that simulate a full proposal → execution flow.

References

  • Microsoft Retrieval‑Augmented Generation concepts: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/retrieval-augmented-generation
  • LoRA: Low‑Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models, arXiv 2106.09685: https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685

End of guide.

title: Crysto: how I run Claude, Codex and other AI models as one team. The models were the easy part.
description:
Early on, two of my AI agents tried to use the same browser at the same time. The browser fell over. Neither of them had really done anything wrong. They had each followed their instructions to the letter. They just had no idea the other one was there.

That was when I realised the hard part of running AI agents isn't the AI. Getting a model to write decent code is close to solved. Getting four of them to work on the same projects for weeks, without stepping on each other, redoing each other's work, or cheerfully telling me something was done when it wasn't, is where all my time has gone.

I call the whole setup Crysto. It started as a way to keep my own projects organised, and grew into something I lean on for my professional work too, with the two sides kept completely separate. Here's how it works, and what broke along the way.

Why I built it

I'm an AI engineer, so I spend most of my day with these tools anyway. But my own projects were scattered: side projects, research, writing and the important things I needed to keep on top of, all half-done across different chat windows. Every new chat started from nothing, and I was the only one keeping track of where anything was up to.

Who's on the team


The Crysto stack. Click through it at vanshaj1999.github.io/crysto

Claude Code runs the show. It plans the work, writes briefs for the others, reviews everything they hand back, and decides what actually ships. I run it on two separate accounts, one for work and one personal, and a small shell hook switches between them depending on which folder I'm in.

Codex gets the long jobs. Give it a clear brief and it will build a small project, or grind through a pile of browser forms, while I get on with something else.

Smaller models, through a tool called OpenCode, handle the bounded fixes. I can hand the same task to five of them at once and keep whichever result is best.

Claude on my phone connects through a small MCP server on Cloudflare Workers, with KV storage behind it. That gives the phone and laptop access to the same stored data without relying on a shared chat.

The coding agents also run headless. These are the command shapes I use, with a model and brief supplied for each run:

opencode run --format json -m <model> "<brief>"

codex exec -s workspace-write "<brief>"

Each run gets its own copy of the repo. OpenCode runs one model per invocation; Codex works inside its workspace-write sandbox. Separate copies matter when I'm comparing results: otherwise a later model could inherit an earlier model's edits, and I'd have no clean way to tell who did what.

The catch is that none of them share a conversation. Everything below comes from that.

Nobody remembers anything

Codex can't see my Claude chats. Tomorrow's Claude session can't see today's. Every agent wakes up with amnesia.

What fixed it was embarrassingly low-tech: files. Every project lives in a folder with a STATUS.md that says where things are up to. Every session reads it first and updates it before it finishes. Longer-term memory is one fact per file with a one-line summary, and only a short index of those gets loaded each time. Each memory file has front matter for its name, description and type. The four types are user, feedback, project and reference. The index tells the agent what exists; it can read the relevant file when the task needs it.

The part that surprised me was how much it helps to give every rule a reason. "Only one agent uses the browser at a time" is a rule. Add "because two agents on the same debugging port will crash each other" and an agent can work out the case I never wrote down, like a second browser tool on the same machine.

It sounds almost too simple to write about. But it's the reason any agent, on any model, can pick up a project cold.

Who's doing what

Back to the browser crash. The fix was one more file, COORDINATION.md, which lives in the hub. Before an agent touches files or the browser, it writes down that it's taking the job:

# Website copy review, 4 November: CLAIMED BY CODEX
Owner: Codex. Claimed 4 Nov 10:05.
Done: 12 of 18 claims checked.
Evidence: drafts/about.md diff.
Next: check the last 6, then hand back to Claude.


A real run: creating a project, then the 17 tests in make check

The rules fit on an index card. Check the file before you start. If someone else has claimed a task, leave it and ask me. Only one agent on the browser. And nothing actually enforces any of it. There's no lock. It works because every agent's instructions tell it to respect the file, and so far they do.

It earned its keep this week. A work session already had the browser, so my personal session switched to a different browser tool instead of grabbing it.

Tests that pass and still lie

The whole setup depends on the smaller models building and Claude reviewing. That only works if the review actually catches things, so I tested it.

The bug was pydynox issue #560. Its MemoryBackend decorator wrapped an async function, but exited its context before the coroutine ran. That's a useful failure to test because returning a coroutine and executing it aren't the same event. The context has to cover the actual async execution.

I gave it to 9 models, with tests I'd written beforehand and kept hidden from them. Eight passed those hidden tests; the fastest finished in 84 seconds. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning passed, but also deleted an existing test. If I'd only read the final test result, I'd have missed that change entirely.

The refactor task was in awslabs/stickler, with a 4,091-test suite. Five models kept it green without editing a test. Flint 40B also ran ruff --fix over 8 unrelated notebooks. Its diff touched 11 files, while the others touched 3. The extra changes weren't necessary for the task, even though the suite still passed.


Photo by Kevin Ku on Unsplash

So now Claude does three things with every change. It writes tests up front that the building agent never sees, runs them afterwards, and reads the whole diff. A green test run tells you the tests passed. That's all it tells you.


The build loop. Interactive version at vanshaj1999.github.io/crysto

Everyone exaggerates a little

When an agent finishes, it writes a handover: what it changed, the proof, what went wrong, and what it didn't get to test. The rule is that "done" means a command ran and the output is in the file. Plans and good intentions don't count.

Even so, claims creep. When the smaller models built my retrieval benchmark, their handover was upfront that one feature, the Claude answer path, had never actually run. Their README still made it sound like part of the results. The review also found a threshold that had been tuned on the very questions it was being scored on. Both are fixed now, and the README says so.

That project, rag-eval-lab, uses 745 Python PEPs split into 17,933 chunks, stored in PostgreSQL with pgvector and an HNSW index. Vector search scored recall@1 of 0.70 against 0.36 for full-text search. Hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion, or RRF, scored 0.66. Here, recall@1 asks whether the expected result came first. Adding another retrieval method didn't automatically improve that score.

Those numbers describe this benchmark. They don't prove that vector search wins on every corpus, and they say nothing about an answer path that never ran. That's the distinction I need the handover and README to preserve.

Claude isn't immune either. While drafting my last article, it wrote that my fixes had been sent to the project maintainers. They hadn't, not yet. We only caught it because the check went back to the actual pull requests.

I've stopped hoping for a model that never overstates things. What I want is a check that doesn't take its word for it.

The rules that weren't about AI

Two of my most expensive lessons had nothing to do with models.

My work and personal Claude accounts are kept apart by separate config folders. But both read the same keychain entry, so logging out of one to switch logs out every session on the machine. Now the shell hook handles the switch and prints a line every time it happens, and I never log out.

The account folders use CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR for Claude and GH_CONFIG_DIR for the GitHub CLI. The hook checks the current directory and selects the matching config. These lines come straight from account-switch.zsh:

autoload -Uz add-zsh-hook
add-zsh-hook chpwd _crysto_claude_account
add-zsh-hook chpwd _crysto_gh_account
_crysto_claude_account
_crysto_gh_account

The chpwd hook runs the account functions when the directory changes. The final calls also select the accounts when the shell starts. Separate config folders solve the selection problem; they don't remove the shared keychain behaviour.

Then the voice assistant. My first design for "Hey Crysto" was a small Cloudflare Worker that called Claude with my subscription login. Anthropic's terms don't allow that: a subscription is for their own apps, and anything running on your own server needs a paid API key. So I split the problem. The part that matters most, Crysto's connection to my data, is built and running: a personal MCP gateway on Cloudflare Workers with OAuth and PKCE, read-only by default, where any write needs my explicit consent. Codex signs in to it and reads my mail, calendar and project data through one endpoint. For voice, I use the Claude app and Siri today. The always-on brain, a model that runs by itself and also runs the lights at home, is designed and waiting. The main thing stopping me is the API bill: I'm not ready to pay per request for a side project yet. Next time I'll read the terms before I draw the diagram.

Under the hood

Crysto is mostly Markdown files and shell commands. Claude Code coordinates the work, while headless OpenCode and Codex runs produce changes for review. Project status and task claims live beside the work, so the next session can read them with ordinary file tools.

The public repo includes a bash script to create a project, plus 17 tests, shellcheck and GitHub Actions CI. The Cloudflare Workers MCP server uses KV for stored state. PostgreSQL, pgvector and HNSW belong to the retrieval benchmark, rather than the coordination protocol. I don't need a database query to find out who owns the browser.

What it costs

Not much beyond the subscriptions I already had. Money isn't really the limit. Attention is, so the whole thing is set up to spend it on briefs and reviews rather than on typing code.

If you want to try this

  • Keep shared state in files, not in chats.
  • Have agents claim work before they start, and give the browser one driver.
  • Write your own tests and keep them away from the agent writing the code.
  • Read every diff, even when it's green.
  • Ask for proof, then check it.


The crysto repo on GitHub

The design, the coordination rules, the templates and a script that sets up a new project are all open source at github.com/vanshaj1999/crysto. My memory, notes and data aren't, and that's on purpose.

Want to click through it yourself? The interactive diagrams are at vanshaj1999.github.io/crysto.

Cover photo by James Harrison on Unsplash.

title: Spatial Memory vs Correction Memory: I Benchmarked Both Against a Plain LLM
description:
Earlier this year I wrote about two small open-source libraries for document extraction. The first, Give Your Document OCR Pipeline a Memory, introduced textract-field-memory, which remembers where fields sit on a recurring layout. The second, Your LLM Keeps Making the Same Extraction Mistake, introduced sample-prompt-correction-memory, which turns a human correction into something the pipeline keeps.

Each post made its own case. Neither one answered the question readers kept asking me: if you can only add one, which one, and what does each actually buy you against a plain LLM?

So I built a small benchmark that runs both mechanisms against the same document stream, next to a no-memory baseline, and measured them on the same five metrics. The short answer is that they are not competitors. One is a cost lever and the other is a quality lever.

TL;DR. On 120 synthetic invoices and forms with Claude Haiku 4.5 on Amazon Bedrock: spatial memory cut LLM calls from 600 to 30 (about 95%) and p50 latency from 3.3 s to a memory read. Correction memory left the call count alone but cut the repeated-error rate from 0.185 to 0.012. Both raised field accuracy from 0.815 to about 0.99.

The setup

Three arms process the identical seeded stream, in the same order.

Baseline. Plain LLM extraction on every field of every document. No memory. This is the reference for cost and for how often a mistake comes back.

+Spatial memory. Models textract-field-memory. For the first three documents of a type, it calls the model and records where each field sits. Once a field's position is stable within tolerance, it reads the value from the learned region and skips the model call.

+Correction memory. Models sample-prompt-correction-memory. It always calls the model. The first time a field comes back wrong, a simulated reviewer corrects it, and the arm stores the correction as a generalizing transform (for example, "undo the day/month swap"), not as a frozen value. Later documents of that type get the transform applied.

The dataset is 120 synthetic documents, 60 invoices and 60 forms, five fields each (invoice number, date, vendor, total, tax). Two fields per type carry a deterministic, systematic error, the kind a stateless pipeline repeats forever: a date with day and month swapped, and an amount with a stray leading digit (12.34 read as 112.34).

The five metrics were written down in a test plan before any run: field accuracy, LLM calls, token cost, latency, and repeated-error rate. That last one is the share of later occurrences of a field that still show the same error after it was first corrected.

The results

Real-model run: Amazon Bedrock, us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0, us-west-2, seed 42.

Arm Field accuracy LLM calls Calls/doc Token cost (modeled) p50 latency p95 latency Repeated-error rate
Baseline 0.815 600 5.00 $0.0556 3,331 ms 5,592 ms 0.185
+Spatial memory 0.990 30 0.25 $0.0028 ~0 ms 156 ms 0.007
+Correction memory 0.988 600 5.00 $0.0556 3,218 ms 4,243 ms 0.012

By document type, the baseline scored 0.80 on invoices and 0.83 on forms. Spatial memory reached 0.99 on both. Correction memory reached 1.00 on invoices and 0.98 on forms.

The cost column is small because the run is small. The ratio is what matters: spatial memory ran at about 5% of the baseline's modeled token cost.

What each number is telling you

Spatial memory is the cost story. The 30 calls it made are exactly the warmup: 3 documents, times 5 fields, times 2 document types. After that, every field on every document was a lookup. That is why p50 latency collapses to a memory read and p95 drops to 156 ms (the tail is the warmup documents). On a stable, high-volume layout, the model is doing work the layout already answered.

Correction memory is the quality story. It does not save a single call, because it still runs the model on every field. What it changes is what happens after the first mistake. In the baseline, the date swap and the stray digit come back on every later document, which is where the 0.185 repeated-error rate comes from. With correction memory, each systematic error is paid for once, by one review, and then it stops. The rate drops to 0.012.

They fix different failure modes. Spatial memory removes redundant calls on fields the layout pins down. Correction memory removes errors the model keeps making on calls that still happen. A pipeline that has both problems needs both layers, and a combined arm is the obvious next configuration to measure.

How this connects the two earlier posts

The OCR memory post ended with a direct ask: the stress tests there were operational numbers, with no labeled benchmark and no comparison against a baseline. This benchmark is a first step on that. It has ground-truth values, a fixed baseline, and pre-registered metrics.

The correction memory post described a three-tier design: graduated rules at zero cost, a confidence-gated LLM tier, and few-shot self-healing for low-confidence fields. This benchmark isolates one property of that design, that a correction applied once stops the same mistake from recurring, and measures it on a stream.

Put together, the two posts describe two separate places a pipeline wastes effort. This post puts numbers on both, side by side.

What this benchmark does not show

These caveats matter more than the headline, so read them before quoting a number.

The arms model the libraries, they do not import them. Each arm is a self-contained reimplementation of the library's core mechanism, so the benchmark runs with no install and no network. The published libraries do more (IoU and center-distance scoring, template identification, drift detection, rule graduation, few-shot retry). Swapping the real libraries into the arms is the next step.

The spatial arm's accuracy is close to an upper bound. When spatial confidence is high, the arm returns the value at the learned position, and on synthetic data that value is the ground truth. In a real pipeline, that read still depends on the OCR being right in that box. The defensible claim from this arm is the 95% call reduction. The accuracy gain says that on a stable layout, a positional read avoids the model's occasional misread, assuming the OCR is clean.

The correction arm knows two error patterns. Its transform learner recognizes the day/month swap and the stray leading digit, because those are the errors the generator injects. A real correction log is messier, and the first post covers how the library handles that with few-shot retrieval instead of hand-written transforms.

The errors are synthetic. In Bedrock mode, the model reads a pre-noised OCR span, so the baseline's errors come from the injected noise model, not from Haiku misreading a clean document. The accuracy and repeated-error deltas are properties of that noise model on this set. Treat them as directional.

Cost is modeled. Measured input and output tokens from the Bedrock usage block, times the published Haiku 4.5 rate ($1.00 per 1M input tokens, $5.00 per 1M output tokens). It is not a bill.

It is small. 120 documents, two types, one seed for the real-model run.

The two mechanisms, in code

The harness is small enough that the core of each arm fits on screen. This is the decision the spatial arm makes for every field:

def confident(memory, key, bbox, warmup=3, tol=0.02):
    """True once a (doc_type, field) has a stable learned position."""
    if key not in memory:
        return False
    learned_bbox, seen = memory[key]
    if seen < warmup:
        return False
    return all(abs(a - b) <= tol for a, b in zip(learned_bbox, bbox))

# per field:
if confident(memory, (doc_type, field_name), field_bbox):
    value = read_region(field_bbox)        # no LLM call
else:
    value = call_llm(field)                # warmup or position moved
observe(memory, (doc_type, field_name), field_bbox)

And this is the correction arm. The important part is that the stored correction is a transform that inverts the systematic error, not the corrected value itself, so it applies to the next document regardless of its specific date or amount:

def learn_transform(raw, truth):
    # Day/month swap: 2026-07-03 read as 2026-03-07
    if raw.count("-") == 2 and truth.count("-") == 2:
        ry, rm, rd = raw.split("-")
        ty, tm, td = truth.split("-")
        if ry == ty and rm == td and rd == tm:
            return lambda v: "-".join([v.split("-")[0], v.split("-")[2], v.split("-")[1]])
    # Stray leading digit: 12.34 read as 112.34
    if "." in raw and raw[1:] == truth:
        return lambda v: v[1:]
    return lambda v: v   # not systematic, do not transform

# per field:
raw = call_llm(field)
if key in corrections:
    value = corrections[key](raw)          # apply what review taught us
elif raw != truth and not reviewed[key]:
    corrections[key] = learn_transform(raw, truth)   # one human review
    reviewed[key] = True
    value = truth
else:
    value = raw

The Bedrock call itself is a single-field Converse request at temperature 0 with maxTokens 64, asking for the value only. Token counts come from the response usage block, which is what drives the cost column.

Rebuilding it yourself

The harness is not public, but nothing in it is hard to rebuild, and the method is the useful part. Generate a few hundred synthetic documents from two or three fixed templates, with ground-truth values and bounding boxes per field. Inject one or two systematic errors per type (a date swap and a stray digit are enough to start). Run every arm over the same seeded stream in the same order, log every field, and compute the metrics from the logs afterwards rather than inside the arms. That last step keeps the arms simple and makes each number auditable against the raw records.

I also ran the same harness with a deterministic stub in place of the model, with no AWS account, to check the metric math. It showed the same structure as the Bedrock run: the baseline at 0.803 accuracy and a 0.197 repeated-error rate, spatial memory at 30 calls and 0.990 accuracy, and correction memory at 1.000 accuracy with no repeated errors. When the stub and the real model agree on the shape, the shape comes from the mechanism and not from one model's behavior.

Where this goes next

Three things are on the list. A combined arm, spatial memory first and correction memory on whatever still reaches the model. The real libraries swapped in for the reimplemented mechanisms. And document types where layouts drift, which is where spatial memory should hand back to the model and where textract-field-memory's drift detection earns its place.

If you run document pipelines and have a layout-heavy, correction-heavy workload, I would like to hear which of the two problems costs you more. That answer decides which layer to add first.

Libraries: textract-field-memory and sample-prompt-correction-memory

title: DSPy: stop hand-tuning prompts, write signatures and let a metric pick the prompt
description:
Thursday AI Tool/Workflow. This week's tool: DSPy, the open-source Python framework from Stanford NLP for "programming, not prompting" language models. You describe a task as typed inputs and outputs, pick a module that decides how the model runs it, and then let an optimizer tune the prompt against a metric you write.

If you've shipped an LLM feature, you know the loop: tweak the prompt, eyeball five outputs, ship, then a model update or a new edge case breaks it and you start again. The prompt is a long string nobody wants to touch, and there's no number telling you whether the last edit helped.

DSPy turns that loop into code you can test. Here's exactly how to use it.

What DSPy gives you

From the official docs, the three pieces that matter:

  • Signatures: declare the task as typed input and output fields (with Literal, Optional, lists, even dspy.Image) instead of writing a prompt.
  • Modules: control how the signature runs. dspy.Predict is a direct call, dspy.ChainOfThought adds step-by-step reasoning, dspy.ReAct adds tools and a reasoning loop. Same signature, different strategy.
  • Optimizers: give DSPy examples and a scoring function and it tunes the prompt (instructions and/or few-shot demos) for you. BootstrapFewShot, MIPROv2 and GEPA all ship in the package.

It's MIT-licensed, and DSPy 3.4.1 (October 2026) on PyPI requires Python 3.10 or newer.

1. Install and connect a model 

pip install dspy

import dspy

lm = dspy.LM("openai/gpt-5-nano", api_key="YOUR_OPENAI_API_KEY")
dspy.configure(lm=lm)

print(lm("What is the capital of France?"))
# ['The capital of France is Paris.']

Models use a "provider/model" string. The docs list native routes for Anthropic (anthropic/...), Google AI Studio (gemini/...), Azure OpenAI, Vertex AI and local Ollama (ollama_chat/llama3.2:1b), plus any OpenAI-compatible server via api_base:

lm = dspy.LM(
    "openai/your-model-name",
    api_base="https://your-provider.example/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_PROVIDER_KEY",
)

dspy.configure(lm=...) sets the default for the whole process. Use with dspy.context(lm=other_lm): to override it for one block.

2. Your first signature

Here's a support ticket classifier. Notice there is no prompt anywhere:

from typing import Literal
import dspy

class TriageTicket(dspy.Signature):
    """Classify a customer support ticket for routing."""

    ticket: str = dspy.InputField()
    category: Literal["billing", "bug", "account", "feature_request"] = dspy.OutputField()
    urgency: Literal["low", "medium", "high"] = dspy.OutputField()

triage = dspy.ChainOfThought(TriageTicket)

pred = triage(ticket="I was charged twice for my subscription this month.")
print(pred.category, pred.urgency)   # e.g. billing high
print(pred.reasoning)                # ChainOfThought adds a reasoning field

The docstring becomes the instruction, the field names and types become the format, and the Literal types tell the model (and DSPy's parser) which values are allowed. For quick experiments you can also write signatures inline as strings, like dspy.Predict("question -> answer").

Want to see what was actually sent to the model?

dspy.inspect_history(n=1)

This prints the full system and user messages plus the raw response. Run it once; it's the fastest way to stop thinking of DSPy as magic.

3. Write a metric and get a baseline

Optimizers need to know what "better" means. A metric is a plain Python function that takes a labeled example and the program's prediction and returns a score (by convention 0.0 to 1.0).

# Labeled tickets: in real life, pull 50-200 from your helpdesk history
rows = [
    ("I was charged twice this month", "billing", "high"),
    ("App crashes every time I log in", "bug", "high"),
    ("Can you add a dark mode?", "feature_request", "low"),
    ("How do I change the email on my account?", "account", "low"),
    # ...
]

examples = [
    dspy.Example(ticket=t, category=c, urgency=u).with_inputs("ticket")
    for t, c, u in rows
]
trainset, devset = examples[: len(examples) // 2], examples[len(examples) // 2 :]

def triage_metric(example, pred, trace=None):
    category_ok = example.category == pred.category
    urgency_ok = example.urgency == pred.urgency
    if trace is not None:            # during bootstrapping: only keep perfect demos
        return category_ok and urgency_ok
    return (category_ok + urgency_ok) / 2

evaluate = dspy.Evaluate(devset=devset, metric=triage_metric, num_threads=4, display_progress=True)
baseline = evaluate(triage)
print(baseline.score)   # percentage, e.g. 50.0

.with_inputs("ticket") tells DSPy which fields go into the program; the rest (category, urgency) are held back as labels for the metric.

4. Optimize

The simplest optimizer, BootstrapFewShot, runs your program over the training set, keeps the traces your metric scores as correct, and puts them into the prompt as demonstrations:

optimizer = dspy.BootstrapFewShot(
    metric=triage_metric,
    max_bootstrapped_demos=4,
    max_labeled_demos=4,
)
optimized = optimizer.compile(triage, trainset=trainset)

print(evaluate(optimized).score)

For bigger gains, the docs now lead with GEPA, which rewrites the instructions using a reflection model. Its metric can return text feedback explaining why a prediction failed, and the reflection LM uses that feedback to write better instructions:

def triage_feedback(example, pred, trace=None, pred_name=None, pred_trace=None):
    problems = []
    if example.category != pred.category:
        problems.append(f"category should be {example.category}, got {pred.category}")
    if example.urgency != pred.urgency:
        problems.append(f"urgency should be {example.urgency}, got {pred.urgency}")
    score = 1.0 - len(problems) / 2
    return dspy.Prediction(score=score, feedback="; ".join(problems) or None)

gepa = dspy.GEPA(
    metric=triage_feedback,
    reflection_lm=dspy.LM("openai/gpt-5.4"),  # a stronger model to write instructions
    auto="light",                              # budget: "light", "medium" or "heavy"
    num_threads=2,
)
optimized = gepa.compile(triage, trainset=trainset, valset=devset)

Per the GEPA guide, trainset feeds the reflective prompt updates and valset selects which candidate compile returns. Keep a separate test set that neither step sees, and score the final program on that.

5. Save, load, ship 

optimized.save("triage_v1.json")

# in your API service
triage = dspy.ChainOfThought(TriageTicket)
triage.load("triage_v1.json")

The JSON holds the program state: the signature instructions, the selected demos, and the DSPy and Python versions it was saved with. Commit it next to your code and review diffs like any other config.

6. Example workflow: re-tuning the ticket router for a cheaper model

This is an example workflow, not a benchmark. Say your helpdesk router runs on a large model and you want to move it to a smaller, cheaper one without losing accuracy.

  1. Freeze the task. TriageTicket stays the same. Only the LM changes.
  2. Build the eval set once. Export 200 resolved tickets with their final category and urgency. Split into train, val and a held-out test set.
  3. Baseline both models. Run dspy.Evaluate on the test set with the large model and the small one (with dspy.context(lm=small_lm):).
  4. Compile for the small model. Run GEPA with the small model as the program LM and the large model as reflection_lm.
  5. Gate the release. Ship triage_small_v1.json only if its test score is at least the large model's baseline. Otherwise keep the old one.
  6. Repeat on every model release. When a new model ships, rerun steps 3 to 5. The docs make exactly this point: you can rerun the optimizer against a new model and immediately see if it's worth swapping in.

The DSPy docs cite production examples of this pattern: Shopify moved a single-prompt GPT-5 task to a small Qwen model optimized with GEPA, reporting a result about 75x cheaper and about 2x more reliable; Dropbox used DSPy optimizers to move to a smaller model and double program accuracy.

Gotchas before you ship

  • The cache will fool you. DSPy caches LM responses in memory and on disk by default, so calling the same program with the same input twice returns the first answer instantly. Great for cost, confusing when you're testing sampling. Use dspy.LM(..., cache=False) or dspy.configure_cache(enable_disk_cache=False, enable_memory_cache=False) when you need fresh calls.
  • Your metric is the spec. The optimizer selects for whatever the metric rewards. A sloppy metric produces a confidently optimized wrong program. Write it like a unit test.
  • Don't optimize on your test set. Train for proposals, val for selection, test for the number you report.
  • Watch optimizer cost. Optimizers call the model many times. Start with auto="light", set num_threads low enough for your provider's rate limits, and turn on dspy.configure(lm=lm, track_usage=True) to see token usage per prediction.
  • Read the prompt. After compiling, run dspy.inspect_history() or open the saved JSON. The optimized instructions are often long; make sure nothing in them leaks data or encodes a bias you don't want.
  • Pin the version. DSPy moves fast (3.3.0 landed in August 2026, 3.4.0 in September, 3.4.1 in October). The saved JSON records the version; pin dspy== in production and re-check the migration notes when upgrading.

Prompts are a parameter, not a source file. Give them a metric and let the computer do the tuning.

References

  • DSPy documentation: https://dspy.ai/
  • DSPy on GitHub: https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy
  • DSPy on PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/dspy/
  • Setting up DSPy (install, LMs, providers): https://dspy.ai/learn/programming/language_models/
  • Metrics and evaluation: https://dspy.ai/learn/evaluation/metrics/
  • Prompt optimizing with GEPA: https://dspy.ai/learn/optimization/optimizers/
  • Cache tutorial: https://dspy.ai/tutorials/cache/
  • DSPy paper (arXiv 2310.03714): https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03714
  • GEPA paper (arXiv 2507.19457): https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19457

How do you decide a prompt change is actually better today: an eval set, or vibes?

title: Claude Reads Screenshots at 2,576px Now. The Same PNG Can Cost 3x the Tokens
description:
• Book: AI That Answers
  • The series: AI in TypeScript — 5 books, from your first LLM call to agents in production — all five here
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

In April, Simon Willison fed one 3456×2234, 3.7 MB PNG screenshot into his Claude token counter. On Claude Opus 4.6 it came to 1,578 tokens. On Opus 4.7 the same file came to 4,744. That is a 3.01x jump for one image, at the same $5 per million input tokens on both models.

Same file, different model. Opus 4.7 accepts images up to 2,576 pixels on the long edge, about 3.75 megapixels, where earlier Claude models shrank anything bigger to fit 1,568. Anthropic's vision docs now put every model from Claude 4.7 on in that high-resolution tier, with no opt-in. If your app sends screenshots, the per-image cost you estimated on an older model can be a third of what the same PNG costs on a current one.

Small images didn't move. In the same post, a 682×318 image cost 314 tokens on 4.7 and 310 on 4.6. The extra cost lives only in big images, and the rule that decides it fits in one line of arithmetic.

Claude bills images in 28-pixel tiles

Claude doesn't price pixels. The vision docs say it cuts the image into 28×28-pixel patches and charges one visual token per patch: ceil(width / 28) × ceil(height / 28). A 1000×1000 image is 36 × 36 = 1,296 tokens.

Then there is a ceiling. Each model has a long-edge limit and a visual-token budget, and an image over either one is shrunk, aspect ratio kept, until it fits:

Tier Models Max long edge Max visual tokens
High-resolution Claude 4.7 and later 2,576 px 4,784
Standard All other models 1,568 px 1,568

The token budget is the limit that bites. Anthropic's coordinates guide says that for nearly all photos and screenshots the token limit sets the final size, not the edge: a 1920×1080 screenshot on a standard-tier model becomes 1456×819, not 1568×882. On a high-resolution model the same screenshot isn't resized at all and costs 2,691 tokens instead of 1,560.

Run Simon's screenshot through those rules with the guide's reference resize function and his numbers line up. On the standard tier, 3456×2234 shrinks to 1372×887: 49 × 32 = 1,568 patches, exactly the budget. On the high-resolution tier it shrinks to 2383×1540: 86 × 55 = 4,730 patches. That ratio is 3.02x against his measured 3.01x. This is my arithmetic, not a measurement; the 10 to 14 tokens his counts carry on top are most likely the rest of the request, which a token counter includes.


Claude bills per square tile, so a longer edge means more tiles on the bill.

Where the /750 shortcut drifts

The older shortcut, still quoted in write-ups like fast.io's, is width × height / 750, which that write-up calls Anthropic's established rule of thumb. Since 28 × 28 is 784, the two agree within a few percent on mid-sized images: a 1000×1000 image is 1,333 by the shortcut and 1,296 by patches. It drifts in three places.

It ignores the ceiling. 3456×2234 / 750 is 10,294 tokens, a number neither tier will ever bill, because the image is shrunk first. That estimate is about 2x too high for a high-resolution model and over 6x too high for a standard one.

It ignores rounding. Patches round up on each axis. 1120×700 is exactly 40 × 25 = 1,000 tokens. Add one pixel to each side, 1121×701, and it becomes 41 × 26 = 1,066. The shortcut moves by about 2.

It doesn't know your model's tier. Same image, same formula, up to 3x apart depending on the model ID in the request.

What doesn't matter at all is file size. Nothing in the formula looks at bytes, and the coordinates guide notes that the token counting endpoint estimates an image's cost from its dimensions without fully processing it. A 3.7 MB PNG and a 300 KB JPEG at the same dimensions cost the same tokens. Compression only changes latency and request size, and the vision docs warn that lossy JPEG or WebP can add artifacts that make text hard to read, which is the opposite of what you want from a screenshot. File size still matters for limits: each image is capped at 10 MB base64-encoded on the Claude API and 5 MB on Amazon Bedrock.

Count it yourself in TypeScript

The token counting endpoint is free, rate-limited per usage tier (5,000 requests a minute on the Start tier), and works with every active model. It only counts images sent as base64, not by URL or file ID. That is enough to print your own table.

The script below uses the Anthropic TypeScript SDK and sharp. It resizes one screenshot to several long edges, counts each on two models, subtracts a text-only baseline so only the image is left, and prints tokens and dollars per thousand images. I haven't run this script myself, so treat the numbers it prints as the source of truth, not the ones in this post.

// count-image.mts
// npm i @anthropic-ai/sdk sharp
// ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... npx tsx count-image.mts shot.png
import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";
import sharp from "sharp";
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const client = new Anthropic();

const MODELS = [
  { id: "claude-opus-4-6", usdPerMTok: 5 },
  { id: "claude-opus-4-7", usdPerMTok: 5 },
];
// long-edge targets in px; 0 = send the original size
const EDGES = [0, 2576, 1568, 1092, 768];
const PROMPT = "What is on this screen?";

const patches = (w: number, h: number) =>
  Math.ceil(w / 28) * Math.ceil(h / 28);

async function count(model: string, png?: Buffer) {
  const text = { type: "text" as const, text: PROMPT };
  const content = png
    ? [
        {
          type: "image" as const,
          source: {
            type: "base64" as const,
            media_type: "image/png" as const,
            data: png.toString("base64"),
          },
        },
        text,
      ]
    : [text];
  const res = await client.messages.countTokens({
    model,
    messages: [{ role: "user", content }],
  });
  return res.input_tokens;
}

Resize with sharp to each target long edge, never upscaling:

async function atEdge(src: Buffer, edge: number) {
  const img = sharp(src);
  if (edge > 0) {
    img.resize({
      width: edge,
      height: edge,
      fit: "inside",
      withoutEnlargement: true,
    });
  }
  return img.png().toBuffer();
}

The main loop counts every size on both models and prints the table:

const src = await readFile(process.argv[2]);
const rows: Record<string, unknown>[] = [];

for (const m of MODELS) {
  const baseline = await count(m.id);
  for (const edge of EDGES) {
    const png = await atEdge(src, edge);
    const meta = await sharp(png).metadata();
    const w = meta.width ?? 0;
    const h = meta.height ?? 0;
    const tokens = (await count(m.id, png)) - baseline;
    rows.push({
      model: m.id,
      sent: `${w}x${h}`,
      kb: Math.round(png.length / 1024),
      predicted: patches(w, h),
      counted: tokens,
      usdPer1k: ((tokens * m.usdPerMTok) / 1000).toFixed(2),
    });
  }
}

console.table(rows);

The kb column will swing a lot between rows and the counted column won't follow it, because bytes aren't in the formula. And predicted is the patch count of the pixels you sent: when counted lands on or near it, Claude saw your image at the size you sent. When counted is well below it, the server shrank the image to its tier's budget, and you paid for pixels you could have dropped yourself. For a 3456×2234 shot on Opus 4.7, the original and the 2,576 rows should both land near 4,730, the size the server shrinks this shot to. A 2576×1665 image is still 92 × 60 = 5,520 patches, over the 4,784 budget.

Pick the size before you ship

Here is what one screenshot's image tokens cost per thousand requests, computed from the docs' token table and each model's list input price. It leaves out your prompt text and the output tokens.

Model Tier Input $/MTok 1920×1080 tokens $ per 1k 3840×2160 tokens $ per 1k
Haiku 4.5 standard $1 1,560 $1.56 1,560 $1.56
Sonnet 4.6 standard $3 1,560 $4.68 1,560 $4.68
Opus 4.6 standard $5 1,560 $7.80 1,560 $7.80
Opus 4.7 high $5 2,691 $13.46 4,784 $23.92
Haiku 5.5 (≤100K prompt) high $0.10 2,691 $0.27 4,784 $0.48
Sonnet 5.5 high $2 2,691 $5.38 4,784 $9.57
Opus 5.5 high $4 2,691 $10.76 4,784 $19.14

The Sonnet rows are the ones to stare at. Sonnet 5.5's input price is a third lower than Sonnet 4.6's, and a 4K screenshot costs about twice as much on it. Each token got cheaper, but the same image now takes about three times as many of them.


Same screenshot, same file: the model's resolution tier decides how heavy the bill is.

If you don't need the extra detail, shrink before you send. Anthropic's docs say it directly: downsample when you don't need the fidelity, and resize yourself to cut latency. Copy resizedSize from the coordinates guide (it ships a TypeScript version) and pin screenshots to the old standard budget on any model:

// resizedSize() is Anthropic's reference function,
// copied from the vision-coordinates guide.
const STANDARD = { edge: 1568, tokens: 1568 };

async function pinToStandard(src: Buffer) {
  const meta = await sharp(src).metadata();
  const [w, h] = resizedSize(
    meta.width ?? 0,
    meta.height ?? 0,
    STANDARD.edge,
    STANDARD.tokens,
  );
  return sharp(src)
    .resize({ width: w, height: h, fit: "fill" })
    .png()
    .toBuffer();
}

Don't do it blind, though. The same docs say the high-resolution tier exists for computer use, screenshot understanding and dense documents, and small text is the first thing a downscale eats. Run your real screenshots through both sizes, check the answers, and only then pick the budget.

Screenshot apps hit a few more rules. A request with more than 20 images triggers a stricter per-image size limit, and the vision docs say to keep both sides at 3,000 px or under to stay clear on every platform. Screenshots returned to the computer use and browser use tools are rejected with a validation error when they exceed the model's limits instead of being downscaled. And if a silent server-side resize would break your pipeline, set "transformations": { "oversized_image": "error" } on the image block: the API, and the token counting endpoint, then reject the image instead of shrinking it, per the coordinates guide.

The habit that saves you is boring. Before a feature that takes screenshots ships, count one real screenshot on the exact model ID you'll deploy, write the per-image number next to the feature, and recount when you switch models.

If this was useful

Per-request token cost is one of the first things a working LLM app has to get right, and it's a big part of what AI That Answers covers: your first LLM app in TypeScript, from prompts and structured output to knowing what each call costs before your users find out for you. If you want the screenshot feature above to ship with a budget instead of a surprise, that book is where I'd start.

It's book one of AI in TypeScript, five books from your first LLM call to agents in production: the whole series is here.

title: Your agent can't read a deprecation page
description:
When a provider retires a model, the notice goes on a docs page written for people. The API keeps answering until the shutdown date, then the model ID just stops working. An agent running on its own has no way to see it coming.

So I built Upstream: it reads the status pages of 40 AI and developer APIs every few minutes, and the deprecation pages of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, Groq and Cohere, and turns them into answers an agent can ask for before it makes a call.

Here's what last week looked like (Oct 26 to Nov 2):

  • 104 status changes across the 40 providers. 54 times something went from operational to degraded or worse.
  • Fireworks AI alone had 16 of those, and every one named a single model (Kimi K3 six times, GLM 5.3 Flash five). 9 were over in 15 minutes.
  • Netlify had two that ran about 9 and 11 hours. OpenAI, Fly.io, Datadog and Anthropic each had 4 or 5.
  • Mistral marked 5 more model IDs deprecated, with shutdown on Apr 30, 2027, and retired one on Oct 31.
  • 9 model IDs shut down in the next 30 days, including five Gemini TTS and live previews on Nov 17 and claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 on Nov 30.

What the agent actually asks, as MCP tools:

  • check_model_deprecation: is this model ID active, deprecated or retired, when does it shut down, and what replaces it, with the exact row from the provider's page.
  • check_api_status: is this provider up right now, and should I retry, wait or switch.
  • list_recent_api_changes and list_providers.

It's free: 50 calls a day with no key, 500 with a free key. There's also a free daily digest of what broke.

Add it with one URL: https://upstream.toolweather.workers.dev/mcp
Docs for agents: https://upstream.toolweather.workers.dev/llms.txt
Digest: https://upstream-api.pages.dev/digest/

What it can't do yet: it only knows what providers publish, so an unannounced model change won't show up, and a "degraded" on a status page doesn't tell you whether your request will fail. If your provider isn't in the 40, tell me which one.

title: A Human Approval Button Is Not a Security Control
description:
A human reviewer can't safely approve an AI agent's action if they only see the action.

They need to see how the agent arrived there.

Consider a hypothetical procurement agent. It receives an email asking to update a supplier's bank details, checks the supplier record, and prepares the change for approval.

The reviewer sees:

Update supplier payment details?

Approve or reject.

That looks like human oversight. It isn't enough.

The reviewer can't tell whether the request came from an authorized contact, whether the supplier record was verified, what evidence the agent used, or whether the agent encountered conflicting instructions along the way.

The approval is attached to an outcome, not to a decision.

That distinction matters because agent failures often happen before the final tool call. A prompt injection in an email, document, or ticket can change what the agent believes it is supposed to do. The final action may look reasonable while the reasoning path is compromised.

The practical control is an approval packet, not an approval button.

Before a reviewer approves a sensitive action, the system should show:

  • Requested intent: What is the agent trying to accomplish?
  • Agent identity: Which agent, workflow, and delegated authority produced the request?
  • Evidence: Which messages, records, or documents influenced the decision?
  • Tool history: What systems did the agent query or modify?
  • Policy result: Which rule allowed the action, and which constraints were checked?
  • Impact: What changes if this is approved?
  • Recovery: Can the action be reversed, and by whom?

The reviewer doesn't need a transcript of every model token. They need the facts that establish accountability.

A useful test for platform teams is simple:

Could a reviewer explain why this action is safe without opening five other systems?

If the answer is no, the control is probably procedural rather than technical. The company has placed a person at the end of an automated workflow, but hasn't given that person enough context to make an informed decision.

This also changes how approval thresholds should work. Low-risk actions can pass automatically when their authority and scope are clear. High-impact actions should pause when the request involves financial changes, external communication, privileged access, or irreversible data operations.

The point isn't to make humans approve more actions.

It's to make each approval meaningful.

An AI agent should present a bounded decision with an evidence trail, not ask a person to bless a conclusion they cannot inspect. That is the difference between human involvement and human control.
