  • You can afford to generate and evaluate several candidate paths.

Don't use when

  • FAQs, simple classification, extraction.
  • Any task where exploring multiple paths is wasteful.

Trade‑offs

Metric ToT
Cost Very High
Latency Very High
Reliability High (for hard tasks)
Complexity High

Prompt ingredients

  • Instruction to generate multiple approaches: "Propose 3 different solutions."
  • Evaluation criteria: cost, risk, performance, maintainability, team skills.
  • Selection step: "Choose the best approach and justify it against the criteria."
  • Clear sections: "Approach 1…", "Approach 2…", "Approach 3…", "Selected approach…"

What to attach

  • Requirements or constraints.
  • Non‑functional requirements (SLOs, compliance).
  • Optional: past decisions and why they succeeded/failed.

Production example

Choosing between event‑driven and request–reply architecture for a new service, with explicit trade‑offs and justification.

💡 Production Tip

Use ToT sparingly for high‑impact decisions. For routine tasks, it's usually overkill.

Pattern 7: Self‑Critique / Reflection

Use when

  • Code review, design review, security‑sensitive outputs.
  • You want a second pass to catch obvious mistakes or style issues.

Don't use when

  • Simple tasks where a single pass is already reliable.
  • You're extremely latency‑sensitive and quality is "good enough".

Trade‑offs

Metric Reflection
Cost High (2+ passes)
Latency High
Reliability High
Complexity Medium

Prompt ingredients

  • First pass: task + constraints.
  • Second pass: "Critique this output against the requirements. List issues, then produce a revised version."
  • Optional rubric: "Focus on correctness, performance, security, readability."

What to attach

  • Requirements / rubric.
  • Coding standards or design guidelines.

Production example

Reviewing an automatically generated API contract or config file to flag versioning, auth, and idempotency issues before committing.

💡 Production Tip

Use self‑critique selectively on high‑risk outputs. Blindly applying it to every call can explode cost without proportional gains.

Pattern 8: Prompt Chaining

Prompt chaining is the practice of splitting one complex prompt into multiple smaller, focused prompts.

Unlike the other techniques, prompt chaining is an orchestration pattern. Instead of changing how one prompt behaves, it changes how multiple prompts collaborate.

Use when

  • One prompt is becoming too large or unfocused.
  • Validation is required between stages.
  • Multiple independent subtasks exist.

Don't use when

  • The task is small and fits cleanly in a single call.
  • You're already latency‑bound and can't afford multiple calls.

Trade‑offs

Metric Prompt chaining
Cost Medium–High
Latency Medium–High
Reliability High (modular)
Complexity Medium

Typical chain 

User Question
      │
      ▼
Extraction
      │
      ▼
Validation
      │
      ▼
Reasoning
      │
      ▼
Formatting

Production example

Natural language → Generate SQL → Validate SQL → Execute → Summarize result.

Many real‑world systems rely on chaining simpler prompts instead of one complex prompt because it's easier to debug, test, and evolve.

💡 Production Tip

Design each step in the chain as its own mini‑API: clear input, clear output schema, and explicit failure modes.

Special case: Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG)

Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) isn't a prompting pattern—it is a context engineering strategy that can be combined with several prompting patterns.

  • Pattern: usually Zero‑shot / Few‑shot / CoT.
  • Context: retrieved documents (chunks, summaries, metadata).

Use RAG when

  • Tasks require knowledge beyond the model's training data.
  • You have a document corpus (docs, tickets, runbooks, knowledge base).

Trade‑offs

  • Extra infra: retrieval, chunking, embedding, versioning.
  • Latency: retrieval + prompt.
  • Reliability: depends heavily on retrieval quality.

Prompt ingredients

  • Role + task.
  • Instructions on how to use retrieved context:
    • "Use only the provided context. If the answer isn't in the context, say so."
  • Retrieved documents or summaries as context.
  • Output format.

What to attach

  • Retrieved chunks (with source IDs).
  • Confidence thresholds and fallback behavior.

Common mistakes

These are the patterns of failure you'll see in real systems:

  • ❌ Using ReAct when no tools are needed.
  • ❌ Adding 20 few‑shot examples instead of improving instructions or schema.
  • ❌ Using Chain‑of‑Thought for simple extraction or classification.
  • ❌ Forgetting schema validation and retry logic.
  • ❌ Dumping entire documentation into the prompt "just in case".
  • ❌ Optimizing prompts before measuring baseline accuracy, latency, and cost.

If you recognize any of these in your system, you've found your next improvement.

How to know when to change patterns

Before switching to a more complex prompting strategy, measure:

Metric Why it matters
Accuracy Is the answer actually correct?
JSON validation rate Does structured output parse reliably?
SQL execution success Does generated SQL run without errors?
Token usage Is the additional context worth the cost?
End‑to‑end latency Does the user experience remain acceptable?
Retry rate Are failures increasing operational cost?

If a simpler pattern consistently meets your quality targets, resist the temptation to introduce more complexity.

Observability matters.

Treat prompts as observable software artifacts. Log prompt versions, context versions, latency, validation failures, and retry counts. Without telemetry, prompt optimization becomes guesswork.

Putting it together: a real production system

A customer support assistant might use:

  • Schema‑driven prompting to produce structured tickets,
  • RAG to retrieve product documentation,
  • ReAct to query account information, and
  • Prompt Chaining to validate the final response before returning it.

Real production systems often combine multiple patterns rather than relying on just one.

Closing: three rules to live by

Production prompting isn't about mastering every technique. It's about choosing the simplest pattern that reliably solves the task, supplying the right context, and validating the output with measurable metrics.

  1. Start simple.

    Use the simplest pattern that satisfies the task and your constraints.

  2. Add context before adding complexity.

    Better schemas, examples, and docs often beat jumping to CoT/ToT/ReAct.

  3. Measure before optimizing.

    Track accuracy, latency, cost, and retry rates. Let data, not hype, drive your prompt architecture.

When you do this consistently, you stop "prompt engineering" in the toy sense and start designing LLM‑enabled systems that are testable, observable, and production‑grade.

Summary visual 

                SIMPLE
                    │
             Zero-shot
                    │
          Schema-driven
                    │
              Few-shot
                    │
        Chain-of-Thought
                    │
                ReAct
                    │
          Tree-of-Thought
                    │
             Prompt Chain
                    │
              Production

References (seminal papers)

  • Wei et al., "Chain‑of‑Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models", 2022. arXiv:2201.11903 [web:51][web:61]
  • Yao et al., "ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models", 2022. arXiv:2210.03629 [web:53][web:56]
  • Yao et al., "Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models", 2023. arXiv:2305.10601 [web:58][web:65]

Further Reading

  • OpenAI Prompting Guide
  • Anthropic Prompt Engineering Guide
  • Google Prompt Design Guide
  • Microsoft Semantic Kernel Prompt Design

title: SaaS MVP Image API Selection: Comparing DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, and Flux for Catalogs
description:
A SaaS MVP should start with the model that preserves the product description most faithfully, then keep the generation boundary replaceable so latency and volume can change the decision later. For messy catalog copy, that usually means starting with DALL-E 3 for prompt adherence, while keeping SDXL and Flux behind the same request shape for the point at which throughput matters more than the last increment of fidelity.

The important design choice is not a permanent model winner. It is a production boundary: text cleanup and policy checks on one side, image generation on the other, with model selection treated as configuration. That lets a small team learn from real catalog fixtures instead of turning an early benchmark into architecture.

Infrai fits this boundary when a team wants a self-describing OpenAI-compatible REST surface for the generation call, plus one key and one billing surface across its backend capabilities. The value here is less vendor loyalty than a smaller handoff: the catalog worker can switch the selected model while discovery supplies schemas and runnable examples.

Should a SaaS MVP use DALL-E for image generation?

Quality comes first when a generated image is the first visual interpretation of a product. A wrong material, color, or use context creates a support problem that a faster response does not fix. DALL-E 3 is the strongest starting point in the supplied comparison for prompt adherence, and its roughly $0.04–0.08 per-image range is a useful order-of-magnitude planning input, not a reason to make price the product decision.

Latency still belongs in the acceptance test. Record the time from an accepted description to a usable image, separate queue time from provider time, and set an SLO for the user-visible workflow rather than pretending that one provider number represents the whole system. A catalog editor can tolerate a background job differently from a checkout preview. Those are different products.

My first capacity question would be blunt: how many descriptions can arrive during the busiest ten-minute window, and how many can the team afford to regenerate? A model choice that looks fine at ten images per hour can become operationally awkward at catalog-import scale. Keep the answer in the workload model, not in a slogan about “real time.”

Where do DALL-E 3, SDXL, and Flux actually differ?

Option Useful first fit Trade-off to validate Boundary condition
DALL-E 3 Ambiguous descriptions where instruction fidelity matters Higher per-image spend than the volume-oriented alternatives Start here when incorrect product attributes are costly
SDXL High-volume generation after the prompt contract is stable Requires more validation that the visual result preserves the catalog intent Prefer it when throughput and repeatability dominate
Flux A middle position between quality and volume, with open-weight availability Open-weight availability does not remove hosting and evaluation work Consider it when deployment control matters enough to justify that work

SDXL is described in the comparison facts as 5–10 times cheaper for volume, while Flux occupies a middle ground with strong quality and open-weight availability. Neither statement answers the production question by itself. A cheap image that needs a human correction is not cheap in the workflow, and an open-weight model still has a capacity plan, a deployment owner, and an evaluation set.

OpenAI is the relevant hosted reference point for DALL-E 3. Stability AI and Black Forest Labs are the names to check when the decision is specifically SDXL versus Flux, while Together AI is another hosted route a team may evaluate for model access. Google Gemini and Anthropic Claude belong on the architecture map for text-side cleanup or review, but they are not interchangeable with the three image-generation choices here. These alternatives need the same fixture set; vendor positioning does not establish their current latency, price, or readiness.

The practical test is a fixed fixture set: the same messy descriptions, the same required attributes, and a review rubric that distinguishes a wrong attribute from an acceptable stylistic variation. Measure quality and queue time together. If the result is a tie, choose the option with the lower integration and operating burden for the current stage.

For example, a description such as “matte black travel mug, leak resistant, fits a car cup holder, shown beside a notebook” should produce a result that preserves the finish, the object type, and the intended context. I would keep those attributes in a small review record rather than asking a reviewer for an overall thumbs-up, because overall approval hides the exact failure that matters to a catalog. A result can look polished while changing matte black to glossy metal or turning a travel mug into a tumbler with a different lid. Run the same record through DALL-E 3, SDXL, Flux, and any hosted alternatives under consideration, then record the first acceptable result, the number of retries, and the time spent waiting. The test should include short descriptions, contradictory descriptions, missing dimensions, and descriptions translated from supplier copy. That is enough to expose prompt sensitivity without pretending to be a universal benchmark. It also gives capacity planning a real input: the worker can estimate how many attempts a catalog import generates, rather than sizing only for the number of source rows.

Do not benchmark only the happy path.

Can one HTTP boundary keep the model decision reversible?

Yes, provided the boundary owns the parts that are genuinely common and leaves model-specific behavior visible in configuration. An OpenAI-compatible /v1/images/generations surface can put DALL-E 3, SDXL, and Flux behind one integration, which is enough to A/B test models without rewriting the catalog worker. The application still needs to store the selected model, request ID, prompt version, and evaluation result; hiding those fields would make later analysis harder, not easier.

The useful advantage of a self-describing API is narrower than “one API does everything.” Discovery can expose the request schema, response schema, billing details, and runnable examples, so wiring a new capability starts with reading the capability description instead of learning another SDK. That is an integration benefit at the provider boundary. It does not turn model evaluation into a solved problem.

Here is the shape I would keep in the worker. It makes retries explicit, does not put a credential in source, and gives a repeated create request a stable idempotency key. The model is data, so moving an experiment from dall-e-3 to an SDXL or Flux identifier does not require a new client path.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type imageRequest struct { Model string `json:"model"`; Prompt string `json:"prompt"` }

func generate(ctx context.Context, model, prompt, requestID string) ([]byte, error) {
    body, err := json.Marshal(imageRequest{Model: model, Prompt: prompt}); if err != nil { return nil, err }
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); if key == "" { return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/images/generations", bytes.NewReader(body)); if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key); req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json"); req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", requestID)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req); if err != nil { return nil, err }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body); resp.Body.Close(); if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 { return responseBody, nil }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("image generation failed with HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, responseBody) }
        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" { if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil { delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second } }
        select { case <-ctx.Done(): return nil, ctx.Err(); case <-time.After(delay): }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("image generation retry loop ended")
}

The code deliberately does not forward the API credential anywhere except the provider request, and it surfaces the response body on failure. In a real worker I would also persist the prompt version and classify a rejected request before retrying; a 4xx response is not a capacity signal. The retry budget belongs inside the job timeout, with the queue treated as at-least-once delivery.

What does the boundary leave out?

A unified generation call does not make every adjacent capability available. Image moderation has no dedicated endpoint in the stated capability set, so a product that needs moderation must put a chat model plus a JSON schema fallback in front of publication and define what happens when the review is inconclusive. Upscaling is limited to Lanczos, which matters if the catalog requires a learned enhancement model rather than a deterministic resize.

That is also the point where I would stop recommending a general boundary and choose a specialist or direct provider. If the workflow depends on a provider-specific control, a particular editing primitive, or a quality characteristic that the common request shape cannot preserve, the abstraction is hiding the decision. Use the direct capability and own the integration deliberately.

For the ordinary MVP path, the boundary is still valuable because the first experiment and the later volume path can share operational code. Use /v1/ai/cost/compare to inspect per-image pricing across available models before committing, and use the model discovery surface to confirm what is ready rather than assuming a model name implies availability. Cost is an input to capacity planning; it is not the acceptance criterion.

The decision rule I would ship

Start with DALL-E 3 when catalog descriptions are inconsistent and a human reviewer will notice wrong attributes. Keep the request contract model-neutral, capture quality and queue-time evidence, and move selected high-volume traffic to SDXL or Flux only after the fixture set shows that the quality loss fits the workflow. Flux deserves the closer look when open-weight availability is a real operating requirement, while SDXL is the clearer volume candidate in the stated comparison.

Infrai is worth trying for the generation boundary when the team wants one self-describing, OpenAI-compatible REST surface to switch among these models without changing the catalog worker, and when runnable discovery examples reduce the time spent wiring a new capability. It is not the right answer for a workflow whose differentiator depends on a provider-specific image operation that the common surface does not expose.

The durable SLO is therefore not “the image API is fast.” It is “a valid catalog description becomes an acceptable image within the editor’s deadline, at the target quality rate, under the peak import load.” That wording forces the team to keep model choice, queue capacity, and human review in the same conversation.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the published capability schema before wiring the worker.

Sources

  • Infrai official documentation
  • OpenAI Batch API guide
  • Cohere Rerank documentation
  • Infrai discovery: ai.batch.submit schema
  • OpenAI image generation guide
  • Stability AI API documentation
  • Black Forest Labs API documentation

title: Akademik Araştırmalarda Veri Güvenliği ve Gizlilik Neden Önemlidir?
description:
Akademik araştırmalar sırasında toplanan veriler, yalnızca bir çalışmanın sonuçlarını oluşturmakla kalmaz; aynı zamanda araştırmaya katılan kişilere, kurumlara ve henüz yayımlanmamış bilimsel çalışmalara ait önemli bilgiler içerebilir. Bu bilgilerin izinsiz paylaşılması, kaybolması veya yanlış kişiler tarafından erişilebilir hâle gelmesi ciddi sorunlara yol açabilir. Bu nedenle veri güvenliği ve gizlilik, araştırma sürecinin her aşamasında dikkate alınmalıdır. Özellikle çevrim içi araştırma ve yazım araçları kullanan öğrencilerin ve akademisyenlerin, İntihal Kontrol gibi platformlara belge yüklemeden önce veri işleme ve gizlilik koşullarını değerlendirmesi önemlidir.

Akademik Araştırmalarda Veri Güvenliği Nedir?

Akademik araştırmalarda veri güvenliği, araştırma sürecinde elde edilen bilgilerin yetkisiz erişime, kayba, değiştirilmesine veya kötüye kullanılmasına karşı korunmasını ifade eder. Bu kapsam yalnızca kişisel bilgileri değil, araştırma sonuçlarını, görüşme kayıtlarını, anket yanıtlarını, laboratuvar verilerini ve henüz yayımlanmamış belgeleri de içerir.

Örneğin, bir araştırmacının katılımcılarla yaptığı görüşmelerin kayıtlarını güvenli olmayan bir ortamda saklaması, bu bilgilere izinsiz erişilmesine neden olabilir. Benzer şekilde, yayımlanmamış bir makalenin kontrol amacıyla güvenilirliği belirsiz bir platforma yüklenmesi, araştırmanın gizliliği açısından risk oluşturabilir.

Bu nedenle veri güvenliği, araştırma tamamlandıktan sonra düşünülecek teknik bir ayrıntı değil, araştırma planının başlangıcından itibaren ele alınması gereken bir sorumluluktur.

Araştırma Sürecinde Gizlilik Neden Önemlidir?

Bilimsel araştırmalar farklı türlerde hassas bilgiler içerebilir. Özellikle insan katılımcılarla yürütülen çalışmalarda kişisel bilgiler, sağlık verileri, görüşler veya özel yaşamla ilgili ayrıntılar toplanabilir. Bu bilgilerin korunması, katılımcıların haklarına ve araştırmacının etik sorumluluklarına saygı gösterilmesi açısından gereklidir.

Gizlilik ilkesi, araştırmaya katılan kişilerin kimliklerinin ve özel bilgilerinin yetkisiz kişilerle paylaşılmasını önlemeyi amaçlar. Katılımcılar, hangi bilgilerin toplanacağını, bu bilgilerin hangi amaçla kullanılacağını ve kimlerin erişebileceğini bilmelidir.

Ayrıca gizliliğin korunması, araştırmaya duyulan güveni de destekler. Katılımcılar bilgilerinin güvenli biçimde işleneceğine inandıklarında araştırmaya daha rahat katkıda bulunabilir. Bu nedenle gizlilik yalnızca yasal veya kurumsal bir gereklilik değil, bilimsel araştırmanın güvenilirliğini etkileyen önemli bir unsurdur.

Akademik Çalışmalarda Hangi Veriler Korunmalıdır?

Araştırmanın konusuna ve yöntemine bağlı olarak korunması gereken bilgiler değişebilir. Anketler, görüşme kayıtları, katılımcıların iletişim bilgileri, deney sonuçları, araştırma notları ve yayımlanmamış makaleler bu kapsamda değerlendirilebilir.

Özellikle kişisel veriler içeren araştırmalarda katılımcıların kimlik bilgilerinin araştırma sonuçlarından ayrı tutulması önemlidir. Örneğin, bir sosyal bilimler araştırmasında katılımcıların isimleri yerine kodlar kullanılması, kimliklerinin doğrudan belirlenmesini zorlaştırabilir.

Bunun yanında, henüz yayımlanmamış araştırma bulguları da korunması gereken bilgiler arasında yer alır. Bu tür belgelerin izinsiz paylaşılması, araştırmacının çalışması üzerindeki kontrolünü kaybetmesine veya araştırma sonuçlarının erken ve bağlamından kopuk biçimde yayılmasına neden olabilir.

Dijital Araçlar Kullanılırken Nelere Dikkat Edilmeli?

Akademik çalışmaların hazırlanması ve değerlendirilmesi sırasında çevrim içi araçlardan yararlanmak oldukça yaygındır. Bulut depolama hizmetleri, belge düzenleme platformları, yapay zekâ uygulamaları ve intihal kontrol programları araştırma sürecini kolaylaştırabilir. Ancak her dijital aracın veri güvenliği yaklaşımı aynı değildir.

Bir platforma belge yüklemeden önce gizlilik politikasını ve kullanım koşullarını incelemek gerekir. Özellikle yüklenen dosyaların ne kadar süre saklandığı, hangi amaçlarla işlendiği ve üçüncü taraflarla paylaşılıp paylaşılmadığı öğrenilmelidir.

Ayrıca platformun sunduğu güvenlik önlemleri, hesap erişimi ve dosya yönetimi seçenekleri de değerlendirilmelidir. Güçlü parolalar kullanmak, ortak cihazlarda oturumu açık bırakmamak ve hassas belgeleri herkese açık bağlantılarla paylaşmamak temel önlemler arasındadır.

Bir aracın ücretsiz veya kolay kullanılabilir olması, verilerin güvenli biçimde işlendiğini tek başına göstermez. Bu nedenle kullanım kolaylığının yanında gizlilik ve güvenlik koşullarına da öncelik verilmelidir.

İntihal Kontrol Araçlarında Belge Gizliliği

İntihal kontrol programları, akademik metinlerdeki olası benzerlikleri belirlemek için kullanılır. Ancak bu araçlara yüklenen belgeler bazen henüz yayımlanmamış tezleri, makaleleri veya araştırma sonuçlarını içerebilir. Bu nedenle program seçerken yalnızca benzerlik tespitinin doğruluğuna değil, belgelerin nasıl işlendiğine de dikkat edilmelidir.

Örneğin, bir öğrenci tezinin tamamını çevrim içi bir platforma yüklemeden önce dosyaların saklanma koşullarını ve gelecekteki kullanımlarına ilişkin açıklamaları incelemelidir. Belgenin kontrol sonrasında silinip silinmediği, bir veri tabanına eklenip eklenmediği veya başka amaçlarla kullanılıp kullanılmadığı önemli sorulardır.

İntihal Kontrol gibi araçları değerlendirirken de platformun sunduğu hizmetlerin yanı sıra gizlilik politikasını ve kullanıcı koşullarını incelemek gerekir. Kullanıcı, yüklediği akademik belgenin nasıl ele alındığını anlamadan yalnızca hızlı sonuç verdiği için bir programı tercih etmemelidir.

İntihal kontrolü, akademik özgünlüğü değerlendirmeye yardımcı olan bir adımdır. Ancak bu işlem sırasında araştırma belgelerinin gizliliğini korumak da aynı derecede önemlidir.

Veri Kaybı ve Yetkisiz Erişim Nasıl Önlenebilir?

Araştırma verilerinin kaybolması, değiştirilmesi veya yetkisiz kişilerin eline geçmesi çalışmanın güvenilirliğini ve devamlılığını olumsuz etkileyebilir. Bu riskleri azaltmak için araştırmacıların düzenli ve güvenli bir veri yönetimi yaklaşımı benimsemesi gerekir.

Önemli belgelerin güvenli yedeklerini oluşturmak, dosyalara erişimi yalnızca gerekli kişilerle sınırlandırmak ve araştırma verilerini düzenli olarak kontrol etmek yararlı uygulamalardır. Özellikle birden fazla araştırmacının birlikte çalıştığı projelerde, kimin hangi belgelere erişebileceğinin önceden belirlenmesi önem taşır.

Dosyaların e-posta veya mesajlaşma uygulamaları üzerinden kontrolsüz biçimde paylaşılması da güvenlik riskleri yaratabilir. Bu nedenle araştırma ekibi, belge paylaşımı için uygun ve güvenli yöntemler belirlemelidir.

Araştırmacıların Veri Güvenliği Konusundaki Sorumlulukları

Veri güvenliği yalnızca kullanılan yazılımların veya dijital platformların sorumluluğunda değildir. Araştırmacılar da topladıkları ve işledikleri bilgilerin korunması için gerekli önlemleri almakla yükümlüdür.

Araştırmanın başlangıcında hangi verilerin toplanacağı, bunların nasıl saklanacağı ve kimlerin erişebileceği belirlenmelidir. İnsan katılımcılarla yürütülen çalışmalarda bilgilendirilmiş onam süreçleri ve ilgili etik kurul gereklilikleri dikkate alınmalıdır. Kişisel verilerin işlenmesi söz konusu olduğunda yürürlükteki veri koruma mevzuatına da uyulmalıdır.

Araştırma tamamlandığında verilerin ne kadar süre saklanacağı ve hangi koşullarda silineceği veya anonimleştirileceği de değerlendirilmelidir. Böylece araştırmacılar hem katılımcıların haklarını koruyabilir hem de bilimsel çalışmaların sorumlu biçimde yürütülmesine katkıda bulunabilir.

Sonuç

Akademik araştırmalarda veri güvenliği ve gizlilik, bilimsel güvenilirliğin ve araştırma etiğinin ayrılmaz parçalarıdır. Katılımcı bilgilerini korumak, araştırma belgelerini güvenli biçimde saklamak ve çevrim içi araçların veri işleme koşullarını incelemek, araştırmacıların dikkat etmesi gereken temel konular arasındadır.

Dijital araçlar akademik çalışmaları daha pratik hâle getirse de bu kolaylık, veri güvenliğinin göz ardı edilmesi anlamına gelmemelidir. Araştırmacılar kullandıkları platformları bilinçli seçmeli ve belgelerini paylaşmadan önce gizlilik koşullarını değerlendirmelidir. Böylece hem kendi çalışmalarını hem de araştırma sürecinde kendilerine emanet edilen bilgileri daha iyi koruyabilirler.

title: Smart Kitchen Gadgets, Home Essentials & Product Discoveries
description:
Discover Smart Products, Everyday Essentials, and Practical Ideas for Better Living
By Kamalendu Hazra

In our busy daily lives, we are always looking for ways to save time, simplify household tasks, and make better choices when shopping online. Sometimes, a small kitchen gadget can make cooking easier. A useful home organiser can help reduce clutter, while a smart household product can make an everyday routine more convenient.

That is the idea behind my YouTube channel, Every Short Useful — helping people discover useful products and practical ideas that can make everyday life a little easier.

Welcome to my world of useful discoveries, smart shopping, and simple living!

A Little About Me

Hello, I’m Kamalendu, the creator behind Every Short Useful.

I believe that useful information does not always need to be complicated or time-consuming. Sometimes, a short video demonstrating a product or explaining its features is all you need to decide whether it deserves a place in your home.

My interest in practical household products, kitchen essentials, smart gadgets, and online product discoveries inspired me to create content that people can explore at their convenience.

My goal is simple: to share helpful product information in an easy-to-understand format so viewers can discover new ideas and make more informed purchasing decisions.

What Is Every Short Useful All About?

Every Short Useful is built around one simple concept: making useful information easy to discover in less time.

Through short-form videos and product-focused content, I aim to introduce viewers to everyday items that may help improve convenience, organisation, and efficiency at home.

Here are some of the topics you can explore.

1. Smart Kitchen Products and Cooking Essentials

The kitchen is one of the busiest places in any home. The right tools can sometimes make everyday cooking and food preparation more convenient.

From vegetable choppers and kitchen scales to storage containers, roti makers, spice organisers, and other cooking accessories, I explore products designed to support everyday kitchen routines.

Whether you enjoy cooking or simply want to make kitchen work easier, these product discoveries can give you new ideas for your home.

2. Home Essentials and Household Gadgets

A comfortable home is not necessarily about expensive furniture or luxury products. Often, it is the small, practical things that make the biggest difference.

My content also explores household essentials such as organisers, cleaning accessories, storage solutions, dustbins, and other everyday products.

The aim is to help viewers discover options that may suit their space, routine, and budget.

3*. Smart Products for Everyday Convenience*

Technology is gradually becoming part of our everyday lives. From digital weighing scales and smart home accessories to innovative household devices, there are many products designed to offer additional convenience.

I enjoy exploring the features of such products and presenting their key details in a simple, accessible way.

Instead of overwhelming viewers with complicated technical information, my approach is to focus on the features that matter when considering a purchase.

4. Practical Product Reviews and Demonstrations

Online shopping offers countless choices, but deciding which product is suitable can sometimes be confusing.

Product-focused videos can help viewers understand important details, including design, specifications, functionality, intended use, and features worth comparing before buying.

I aim to make this information easy to follow.

Remember, however, that a product that works well for one household may not be the right choice for another. Your needs, available space, budget, and expectations should always guide your decision.

Why I Believe Short Videos Are Useful

We all have busy schedules. Not everyone has the time to read lengthy product descriptions or watch a 20-minute review before making a small purchase.

That is where short videos can help.

A well-planned short video can introduce a product, highlight its key features, and give viewers a quick overview of what to consider.

I aim to make every video meaningful, informative, and easy to understand.

Less searching, clearer information, and smarter decisions — one useful discovery at a time.

Helping You Make More Informed Shopping Decisions

I believe that good product content should do more than simply show an attractive item.

It should encourage viewers to look beyond the packaging and consider what really matters.

Before purchasing a product, I recommend checking:

Product features: Understand what the item actually offers.

Specifications: Check dimensions, capacity, materials, compatibility, and other relevant details.

Customer reviews: Read a range of recent reviews to understand other buyers' experiences.

Price and value: Compare prices and features instead of choosing based on discounts alone.

Warranty and support: Review the seller's terms, warranty conditions, and return policy.

Your personal needs: Consider whether the product solves a real problem for you.

I hope that the content I create will encourage viewers to shop thoughtfully rather than buy something simply because it looks interesting.

My Approach to Content Creation

Creating useful content is about more than uploading videos. It is about understanding what viewers want to learn and presenting information in a way they can use.

I aim to keep my content simple, engaging, and relevant to everyday life.

I also recognise the importance of being transparent. Product specifications, prices, availability, and features can change, so viewers should check the latest information on the relevant product page before purchasing.

I do not want viewers to feel pressured into buying anything. I want them to have useful information that helps them decide for themselves.

Building trust takes time, and I believe honest communication is an important part of that journey.

Who Should Follow Every Short Useful?

My channel may be particularly helpful for:

  • People who enjoy discovering practical kitchen gadgets.
  • Families looking for useful home and household essentials.
  • Online shoppers interested in comparing everyday products.
  • People who appreciate quick product introductions and demonstrations.
  • Viewers searching for ideas to organise their homes and simplify daily routines. -Anyone who enjoys discovering interesting and potentially useful products.

Whether you are setting up a new kitchen, organising your home, or simply curious about an innovative household gadget, I invite you to explore the content and decide what is useful for you.

Join Me on This Journey

Every Short Useful is a continuing journey of learning, exploring, and sharing useful discoveries.

I know that no single product or video can solve every problem. However, I believe that small improvements, made one step at a time, can make everyday routines more manageable.

Your suggestions, questions, and feedback can also help shape future content. If there is a kitchen gadget, household essential, or everyday product you would like me to explore, feel free to share your ideas through the channel.

Thank you for taking the time to learn about my work and the purpose behind Every Short Useful.

Visit My YouTube Channel

Explore practical products, discover everyday essentials, and join the community.

👉** Watch Every Short Useful on YouTube:**
https://www.youtube.com/@kamalendu-hazra

If you find a video helpful, consider liking it, sharing it with someone who might benefit, and subscribing for more product discoveries and useful ideas.

Let's make everyday life a little simpler, one useful short at a time!

Life is a Journey — make every discovery count.

Affiliate Disclosure

Some product links shared alongside my content may be affiliate links. If you purchase through qualifying links, I may earn a commission at no additional cost to you. This helps support future content creation.

I encourage viewers to review product details, compare alternatives, and make purchasing decisions based on their own requirements.

AI Content Disclaimer

Artificial intelligence tools may assist with certain aspects of content creation, such as drafting scripts, preparing visual concepts, editing, or improving presentation. AI-assisted content is intended to provide general product information and should not be taken as proof of personal product testing or hands-on experience unless explicitly stated.

Viewers should verify important product specifications, claims, and safety information using reliable sources before making a purchase.

title: Agent frameworks 2026 — LangGraph vs CrewAI vs AutoGen
description:
Three AI agent frameworks have survived the shakeout of 2024-2025 and now dominate production builds in late 2026: LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen. Each solves the same problem — turning an LLM into a system that reasons, calls tools, and iterates — but each takes a sharply different stance on how the agent should be structured, debugged, and scaled.

Teams starting an agent project in 2026 pick between these three (and occasionally lower-weight entrants like Microsoft Agent Framework or OpenAgents). The choice shapes everything downstream: how a stuck agent gets debugged, how long-running workflows survive a server restart, how the team adds a new tool without rewriting the pipeline. This article walks each framework honestly, including the parts the vendor-marketing comparisons gloss over.

The three in one sentence each

  • LangGraph — stateful graph of nodes with explicit edges and checkpointing. Highest control, most boilerplate, best for production.
  • CrewAI — role-based agents working as a crew with task assignments. Fastest to prototype, limited production control.
  • AutoGen — multi-agent conversation framework. Best when the product itself is agents talking to agents. Microsoft moved it to maintenance mode in late 2025; the successor is Microsoft Agent Framework (GA April 2026), and the community fork is AG2 (details below).

LangGraph

LangGraph models an agent as a directed graph. Each node is a function (an LLM call, a tool invocation, a conditional router); each edge is a transition rule. State flows explicitly between nodes and is persisted at every "super-step" via a checkpointer, which means a crashed workflow resumes from the last checkpoint instead of restarting from scratch.

Where LangGraph wins:

  • Deterministic execution + state persistence. The checkpointer is the feature that makes LangGraph the production default. Long-running workflows (minutes or hours), human-in-the-loop approvals, and multi-day agents all survive restarts, deploys, and transient crashes.
  • Explicit control flow. Every path through the agent is a defined edge. Debugging means tracing the graph, not reading agent transcripts hoping to find where the model went off the rails.
  • Human-in-the-loop. The interrupt() primitive (stable since v1.0) pauses a workflow for human approval mid-run without hacks or external queues.

Where LangGraph loses:

  • Steep learning curve. Defining every node, every edge, and every routing function is more boilerplate than CrewAI for simple workflows. A "research agent that searches and summarises" is maybe 20 lines in CrewAI and 80-100 in LangGraph.
  • LangChain lineage. LangGraph lives under the LangChain umbrella. Teams that migrated away from LangChain for complexity reasons may inherit the same complexity here.

Pick LangGraph when: the workflow is longer than one LLM round-trip, has conditional branching, needs retries or approvals, or must survive process restarts.

CrewAI

CrewAI models an agent as a role (a researcher, a writer, a reviewer) with a specific goal and backstory, plus a set of tools. Multiple roles together form a crew that completes tasks in sequence or in parallel. The abstraction is deliberately simple — the framework hides the orchestration mechanics.

Where CrewAI wins:

  • Fast to prototype. A functioning multi-agent demo is possible in under an hour. Role, goal, task — three concepts and the agent runs. For stakeholder demos or "will this even work" exploration, CrewAI is the fastest path.
  • Role-based thinking matches how teams explain workflows. "A researcher agent that finds sources, a writer agent that drafts, a reviewer agent that checks" is easy to design and communicate.
  • Growing ecosystem. By mid-2026 the CrewAI community has shipped templates for common patterns (content review, research synthesis, customer support triage) that get a team from zero to running fast.

Where CrewAI loses:

  • No built-in checkpointing for long-running workflows. A crewed task that runs 20 minutes and fails at minute 18 starts over.
  • Limited control over agent-to-agent communication. The framework decides routing based on roles and task descriptions; teams needing fine-grained control over who-talks-to-whom-when hit the ceiling of the abstraction.
  • Debugging is harder. When the writer agent disagrees with the reviewer and the final output is wrong, the only trail is the agent transcript. There is no explicit graph to inspect.

The migration path that shows up in multiple field reports: teams start with CrewAI for the demo, then migrate to LangGraph when the system needs production-grade state management and conditional routing. The CrewAI code does not translate directly, so plan for a rewrite if that migration happens.

Pick CrewAI when: the goal is a prototype or an internal tool, the workflow fits a role-based mental model, and production reliability matters less than speed of iteration.

AutoGen — status caveat first

Microsoft's AutoGen is where multi-agent conversation frameworks began. The model is simple: define several agents, let them message each other in a group chat, each contributing when relevant. The orchestration emerges from the conversation itself.

The status question that must be answered before picking it in 2026: Microsoft moved AutoGen to community-managed maintenance mode in late 2025, with its last feature release in September 2025. Microsoft's intended successor, Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF), reached general availability on April 2, 2026, combining AutoGen's multi-agent orchestration with Semantic Kernel in a single SDK. A separate community fork, AG2, is independently developed by AutoGen's original authors and continues to ship new features. Before committing to AutoGen for a new production system, decide whether to track MAF, stay on AutoGen-maintenance, or switch to AG2 — each is a different long-term bet.

Assuming AutoGen is still viable for the target workload:

Where AutoGen wins:

  • Conversation-driven workflows. When the product itself is agents debating, reviewing each other's work, or exploring a problem through dialogue, AutoGen's model fits natively. Code review agents, research-and-critique agents, multi-expert simulations.
  • Group chat semantics. AutoGen's GroupChat abstraction captures messy, non-linear agent interaction cleanly. LangGraph can model this but with more effort; CrewAI's role model does not fit.

Where AutoGen loses:

  • Unbounded loops cost money. Without hard termination conditions, open-ended agent debates can consume 5-10× the expected tokens. Every production AutoGen deployment needs a strict max_turns or a budget-based terminator.
  • Debugging a group chat gone wrong. When four agents produced 30 messages and the final output is wrong, root-causing is harder than in a graph or role-based system.
  • The status question. Even if AutoGen is maintained, the ambiguity itself is a reason to think twice for a long-horizon production bet.

Pick AutoGen when: multi-agent conversation IS the product (not a means), the organisation accepts the maintenance uncertainty, and strict termination conditions are built in from day one.

The decision matrix

Need Pick
Long-running production workflow with retries + human approval LangGraph
Fast prototype of a multi-step agent for a stakeholder demo CrewAI
Agents literally talking to each other as the product mechanic AutoGen (after verifying support status)
Deterministic, debuggable, auditable control flow LangGraph
Role-based task delegation, teams can explain the design to non-engineers CrewAI
Code review / expert simulation / debate-driven workflows AutoGen
Must survive process restart mid-workflow LangGraph
Prototype first, migrate to LangGraph later when scaling CrewAI → LangGraph migration path

Cost — be sceptical of per-framework numbers

Several comparison articles publish "framework X uses N× more tokens than framework Y" tables without disclosing their test workload. These numbers are mostly noise:

  • Model choice (GPT-5-mini vs Claude Opus) swings cost 10-20×. Framework contributes <2× at most.
  • Prompt caching usage (see prompt caching article) swings cost 2-10×. Framework-level loops do not affect this.
  • Loop termination logic matters more than framework. An AutoGen group chat with max_turns=3 costs less than a LangGraph loop with no bound.

The honest framing: framework token overhead is real but is almost always dominated by model choice and prompt design. Pick the framework for the control-flow fit; manage cost through model routing and caching at the LLM call layer.

Three failure modes to design around

1. Unbounded loops. Any agent that can call itself (or exchange messages with another agent) needs a strict loop termination condition. "Keep going until the task is done" is not safe. Pick either a max_iterations cap, a token-budget cap, or a hard timeout.

2. State loss on deploy. Agents that run minutes or hours break on every deploy without checkpointing. LangGraph's checkpointer solves this natively; CrewAI and AutoGen users must build their own state persistence or accept that long-running jobs will restart.

3. Debugging without a trace. All three frameworks support tracing (LangSmith for LangGraph/CrewAI; MLflow for AutoGen; OpenTelemetry everywhere). Enable tracing from day one — not day 100 when the first production incident lands. The cost of enabling it later is reproducing bugs you no longer have the state to reproduce.

Three mistakes to avoid

Mistake 1 — Picking by GitHub stars. All three frameworks have >20K stars by late 2026. Popularity does not predict fit for a specific workload.

Mistake 2 — Treating LangGraph as a drop-in CrewAI replacement. The abstractions are different. Code does not port. Plan for a rewrite if a migration happens.

Mistake 3 — Expecting agents to be reliable without evals. All three frameworks produce agents whose output quality depends on prompt engineering and model choice. Build an eval set BEFORE scaling, not after. The RAG evaluation article covers the pattern; agent evals are a close cousin.

Bottom line

For a 2026 agent project starting fresh:

  • If production reliability matters and the workflow is non-trivial: LangGraph. The boilerplate pays for itself the first time a workflow crashes and resumes cleanly.
  • If the goal is a demo or an internal tool: CrewAI. Fastest to running agents, with the understanding that a rewrite may follow.
  • If multi-agent conversation IS the product: Microsoft Agent Framework (the Microsoft-supported path) or AG2 (the community-maintained fork of AutoGen) — plain AutoGen is maintenance-only.

The frameworks will keep evolving. The underlying skills — defining state, bounding loops, instrumenting with traces, running eval sets — transfer across all three.

Related reading:

  • MCP explained — how LLM apps talk to tools in 2026 — the standard for tools these agents call
  • Prompt caching — the LLM discount most teams aren't using — single biggest cost lever for agent workloads
  • Build a RAG pipeline from scratch — RAG is one tool agents commonly call
  • Evaluating RAG — retrieval + generation metrics — the eval harness pattern that extends to agent evals
  • Claude API vs OpenAI API — developer perspective

Originally published on aiunplugged.in.

title: Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base: A 280B Open-Weight Model You Can Fine-Tune — Explained Honestly
description:
Nothing here is sponsored — no affiliate links on this page. This breaking article is not the daily buyer-intent post. Facts below come from the sources listed at the end, checked 5 November 2026. We have not tested ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base hands-on, and nothing here is a hands-on finding.

Baidu has released a serious research artefact, and the honest way to describe it is also the least exciting-sounding one: a base model. On 5 November 2026, Baidu's ERNIE Team announced ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base — a text-only mixture-of-experts model with 280 billion total parameters and 14 billion activated per token, with downloadable weights. The checkpoint ends at pre-training. There was no mid-training and no post-training. That is the point of the release, not a flaw in it — and it changes everything about who this model is for.

If you were hoping for a new chatbot to try this afternoon, stop here: this is not that. If you fine-tune models, run training research, or build on top of open weights, this is one of the most interesting releases of the month. The rest of this article is about why, and about the licence trap that could matter more than any benchmark.

How we put this together

We verified the story against the 5 November 2026 coverage — Unite.AI's report on the release, Artiverse's analysis, and the underlying model card and repositories they cite — keeping every benchmark claim labelled as Baidu's own and every licence condition tied to the licence text as reported. We have not run ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base ourselves, so nothing here is a hands-on finding. Where the announcement gives no number or date, we say so.

Verdict

ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base is a genuinely valuable release for researchers and fine-tuners: a large, modern MoE base model with downloadable weights, strong self-reported exam and coding scores, and a 1-million-token context ceiling. But it is a base model, not a product — it will not chat with you out of the box — and its custom licence is the real story for anyone building commercially: the EU, UK and South Korea are excluded entirely, and commercial use above $50 million in related annual revenue needs Baidu's written permission. Read the licence before you download the weights. The model is free to look at; it is not free of conditions.

What it is

ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base is a text-only mixture-of-experts (MoE) base model. The two numbers that matter most are 280 billion and 14 billion: 280 billion total parameters, of which only about 14 billion are activated per token. That is the whole MoE bargain — a huge reservoir of specialised knowledge, with only a small slice doing work on any given token, which keeps inference costs far below what a dense 280-billion-parameter model would demand.

The architecture, as listed on the model card, is 43 layers with a hidden size of 4,096 and 64 attention heads. Two design choices are worth understanding even if you never touch the weights. First, 37 of the 43 layers use Heavily Compressed Attention: their cache holds one entry for each 128-token block, plus a short window of recent uncompressed tokens, while six Multi-head Latent Attention layers keep token-level access to the full context and use an indexer to pick the highest-scoring earlier positions. Baidu says this sparse selection keeps per-query core-attention cost constant as context grows — which is the engineering behind the long-context claim below. Second, every layer except the first uses an MoE block with 512 routed experts, of which 10 are activated, plus one shared expert. The experts operate in a 2,048-dimensional latent space rather than the model's full hidden width, which Baidu says roughly halves expert dispatch and combination traffic and expert FLOPs relative to full-width experts. The design also includes four parallel residual streams through manifold-constrained hyper-connections and a MultiMax output head with a learnable piecewise temperature. You do not need to memorise any of that. What it adds up to is a model built, from the ground up, to keep the cost of very long inputs under control.

Pre-training ran on 33.5 trillion tokens, using the Muon optimizer and FP8 mixed precision. The training context was gradually extended to 128K tokens, and fine-tuning and inference support up to 1 million tokens. The corpus is worth a look too, because it tells you what the model was built for: alongside multilingual web data it includes code and records of software development — commits, issues, pull requests, reviews, generated tests and CI-verified fixes — plus curated long documents, sequences with semantically similar distractors, and synthetic retrieval and question-answering data for long-context training. That is a corpus aimed squarely at repository-level reasoning, agentic software engineering and extended inputs. It is not a general chatbot diet. It is a working diet.

And the checkpoint itself is the key fact of this release: it ends at pre-training, before mid-training or post-training. Baidu is explicit that this gives developers a common starting point for domain adaptation, instruction tuning and reinforcement-learning research — and a fixed baseline for controlled comparisons of training methods. In other words, the value here is reproducibility. Everyone who fine-tunes this checkpoint starts from exactly the same place, and can compare methods against each other honestly. That is a genuinely useful thing for the research community, and it is also why this release will barely register with ordinary users: there is no chat interface, no instruction following, no alignment. A base model completes text. It does not answer your questions politely.

The headline numbers — labelled as Baidu's own

Baidu evaluated ERNIE against the publicly released DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base, Hy3-preview-Base and MiMo-V2.5-Base checkpoints using the same harness, the same prompts and few-shot examples, and the same LLM judge for free-form question answering. That is the right way to run a comparison, and it is worth saying so — but it is still Baidu's harness, Baidu's table, and Baidu's numbers. No independent lab has reproduced them yet.

Here is what the table shows, selected results:

  • MMLU, five-shot: ERNIE 93.3 — DeepSeek V4 Flash 89.4, Hy3 preview 87.5, MiMo V2.5 87.6
  • HumanEval+, one-shot Pass@1: ERNIE 82.3 — DeepSeek V4 Flash 69.5, Hy3 preview 78.0, MiMo V2.5 74.4
  • FullStackBench, one-shot Pass@1: ERNIE 54.6 — DeepSeek V4 Flash 43.3, Hy3 preview 56.7, MiMo V2.5 54.1
  • InfiniteBench, zero-shot average: ERNIE 46.5 — DeepSeek V4 Flash 48.0, Hy3 preview 33.0, MiMo V2.5 46.7

Read that as it is: a strong showing, not a clean sweep. ERNIE leads clearly on MMLU — a broad exam-style knowledge test — and on HumanEval+, a coding test, where its 82.3 against DeepSeek's 69.5 is a wide margin. But Tencent's Hy3 leads on FullStackBench, a broader coding benchmark, and DeepSeek leads on InfiniteBench, the long-context test — which is a little ironic, given how much of this model's design is aimed at long context. The honest summary is that ERNIE looks strong on exams and on single-function coding, competitive elsewhere, and not dominant across the board. Anyone reporting only the MMLU number is selling you a headline. The full table is the story.

One more caution about that MMLU figure: 93.3 is very high, and high MMLU scores on base models should always invite the same question — how much of it is the model, and how much is the evaluation setup? We cannot answer that from Baidu's table alone. Independent runs will tell. Until then, treat 93.3 as a claim to be checked, not a fact to be quoted.

What you can actually use today

The weights are downloadable in FP8 and BF16 safetensors formats. The model card documents production serving with SGLang and vLLM through the completions API — note: the completions API, matching the checkpoint's base-model status, not a chat API. The accompanying FlashMask repository documents attention kernels for Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, with Blackwell configurations supporting head dimensions up to 576 for query and key and 512 for value. Baidu reports speed gains of up to 175% in the forward pass and 74% in the backward pass over FlashAttention-4 MaskMod on SM100 hardware — Baidu's own figures, on Baidu's chosen comparison, so take the size of the gain with the usual pinch of salt while noting the direction is plausible for a purpose-built kernel.

There is also a practical on-ramp for fine-tuning: NVIDIA's Megatron Bridge recipe adds a supervised fine-tuning workflow covering data preparation, training and export back to Hugging Face format. Its full-model recipe uses 16 nodes with four GB300 GPUs per node, and NVIDIA validates the recipes on Blackwell GB200 and GB300 systems — the components support Hopper, but Hopper is not validated. Read that hardware line twice before planning a project around this model. A 280-billion-parameter model, even with only 14 billion active per token, is not a weekend laptop project for full fine-tuning. The weights are downloadable; running them well is a serious infrastructure commitment. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning may be the realistic route for most teams, and nothing in the sources for this article states a LoRA or adapter recipe, so we will not invent one.

Baidu says a post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash will follow this base version. No date has been given in the sources for this article. When it arrives, that is the version ordinary users and most developers will actually want — the one that follows instructions and chats. This base release is the foundation, not the house.

The licence trap — read this before you download

This is the section that matters most, and the one most coverage will bury. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base is not released under Apache 2.0, MIT or any standard open licence. It is released under a custom ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base Model License Agreement v1.0, and its conditions are strict in ways that will exclude a large share of potential users outright.

  • Territory: the licence's territory excludes the European Union, the United Kingdom and South Korea. Use, modification and distribution outside the licensed territory are not authorized. If you are in the EU, the UK or South Korea, this model is, on the face of the licence, not for you.
  • Commercial use up to $50 million: non-commercial use is free of model licence charges. Commercial use at or below $50 million in annual revenue from related products or services requires a one-time notice and prominent "Powered by ERNIE" attribution.
  • Commercial use above $50 million: above that threshold, you need Baidu's separate prior written authorization. That is a negotiation, not a download.
  • Distillation and synthetic data: the agreement bars using the licensed materials, derivative models or their outputs to improve an unrelated AI or machine-learning system. That restriction matters for distillation and synthetic-data workflows, which the licence expressly addresses when defining derivative models and limits on output use. If your plan was to use ERNIE's outputs to train a smaller model, stop and read the licence first.

Put plainly: "downloadable weights" and "open" are not the same thing, and this release is the proof. Compare it with the recent open-weight releases that shipped under Apache 2.0 with no territorial carve-outs — this one is a different animal. For researchers inside the licensed territory doing non-commercial work, the conditions are light. For a European startup, a UK lab, a Korean company, or any business that might one day cross $50 million in related revenue, the conditions are a wall. That does not make the release worthless. It makes it conditional. Know which side of the conditions you are on before you invest weeks of fine-tuning work on top of a checkpoint you may not be allowed to ship.

Why it matters

Three things make ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base worth attention even before independent verification. First, a fixed, downloadable, pre-training-only checkpoint at this scale is genuinely useful infrastructure for research: it lets the community test training methods, alignment techniques and long-context approaches against a common starting point, without anyone having to repeat a 33.5-trillion-token pre-training run. Second, the architecture is a serious attempt at the problem every frontier lab is wrestling with — how to make very long context affordable — and the combination of compressed attention, latent-space experts and a purpose-built kernel is a design worth studying whether or not you ever run the model. Third, the release sharpens a question the open-weight world has been avoiding: what "open" means when the licence carries territorial exclusions and revenue gates. Each release like this forces the community to be more precise about the difference between downloadable weights and genuinely open weights. That precision is overdue.

Who it matters for

  • Researchers in training methods and alignment. A fixed base checkpoint at 280B scale, with a documented training recipe lineage and a post-trained version coming, is exactly the baseline you want for controlled comparisons. Check the licence territory first.
  • Teams fine-tuning for code and agentic software engineering. The corpus is built for repository-level work, the HumanEval+ number is strong, and SGLang/vLLM serving plus a Megatron Bridge SFT recipe give you a real starting point — if you have the hardware and the licence allows your use.
  • Developers who just want a model to chat with. Wait for the post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash. This base checkpoint will not do that job.
  • Anyone in the EU, UK or South Korea, or building a commercial product that may cross $50M in related revenue. Read the licence before anything else. The territorial exclusion and the written-authorization threshold may rule this model out for you entirely.
  • Anyone tracking the open-weight race. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base is another data point that the race is no longer just about parameter count: training data composition, attention design for long context, and — increasingly — licence terms matter as much as size.

The limits — stated plainly

  • This is a base model, not a finished assistant. No instruction tuning, no alignment, no chat behaviour. It completes text; it does not follow instructions.
  • All benchmark claims are Baidu's own, with no independent verification yet. MMLU 93.3 and HumanEval+ 82.3 are self-reported, and the comparison is task-dependent — Hy3 leads on FullStackBench, DeepSeek leads on InfiniteBench.
  • The licence is custom and restrictive. EU, UK and South Korea excluded; commercial use above $50 million in annual related revenue needs Baidu's prior written authorization; outputs may not be used to improve an unrelated AI system. This is not Apache 2.0.
  • Full fine-tuning needs serious hardware. NVIDIA's full-model SFT recipe uses 16 nodes with four GB300 GPUs each, validated on GB200/GB300; Hopper is supported but not validated.
  • The post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash has no date. Baidu says it will follow; no date has been given in the sources for this article.
  • The 1-million-token context applies to fine-tuning and inference, not to pre-training, which extended to 128K tokens. Treat hosted long-context behaviour as claimed until providers confirm it.
  • No hands-on testing was performed for this article, and no benchmarks, prices or dates have been invented.

The bottom line is a measured one. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base is a serious, useful release for the people it is actually for — researchers and fine-tuners working inside its licence territory, with the hardware to run a 280-billion-parameter model and the patience to build on a raw checkpoint. Its exam and coding numbers are loud, its long-context engineering is thoughtful, and its fixed-baseline approach is genuinely good for science. But the licence is the story: a model that excludes the EU, the UK and South Korea, gates large-scale commercial use behind Baidu's written permission, and restricts distillation is not "open" in the way most developers mean the word. Download the weights if the terms fit you. If they don't, admire the engineering from a distance — and wait for the post-trained version, or for a release whose licence matches its ambitions.

Sources: Unite.AI, "Baidu Releases ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base for Further Training", 5 November 2026; Artiverse, "Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Base Targets Serious Model Research"; Baidu ERNIE Team announcement and model card; FlashMask repository; NVIDIA Megatron Bridge recipe; ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base Model License Agreement v1.0. Benchmark figures are Baidu's own, as reported in the coverage. No hands-on testing was performed for this article. This breaking article is not the daily buyer-intent post, and it contains no affiliate links.

Originally published at ToolsDig

title: How Fusion works: DeepSeek V4 Pro plans, V4 Flash writes the code
description:
Big models write better plans. Small models are cheaper and fast enough to type the code. I wanted both in one session without switching models by hand.

That's Fusion. It's one entry in FreePi, a free AI coding agent for the terminal. This post explains how it splits a task between DeepSeek V4 Pro and DeepSeek V4 Flash, how the switch happens, and when it's worth turning on. Everything here comes from the code that ships in the CLI today.

Try it: run npx free-pi-cli@latest in a terminal, then pick Fusion in /model.

Give this to your agent: freepi.ai/llms.txt

The short version

Every message you send goes through three phases:

  1. Explore. DeepSeek V4 Flash reads your code with read-only tools. It makes no edits.
  2. Plan. DeepSeek V4 Pro gets one request. It writes a step-by-step plan into the agent's todo list. It can't edit files.
  3. Build. Flash takes over again. It works through the todo list, edits files and runs tests.

So Pro answers one request per message. Flash handles every other request, including all the follow-ups after tool calls.

How you turn it on

FreePi runs the pi coding agent. Type /model and Fusion is the first entry in the list. Pick it, and the footer shows Fusion plus the model that answered the last request.

Fusion isn't the default. A new session starts on the default model the server lists first, so you pick Fusion yourself.

Fusion is a router, not a model

pi has a feature called virtual models. A virtual model shows up in /model like any other model. Before every request, it runs a route function that picks a real model to send that request to.

Fusion is a virtual model. When you pick it, nothing new runs on the server. Each request still goes out as a normal request to deepseek-v4-pro or deepseek-v4-flash.

The router keeps one piece of state per session branch, the current phase. Here's the core of it, trimmed, with one helper renamed:

switch (request.reason) {
  case "user":
    // a new message from you: start over
    return route(executor, "explore");
  case "continuation":
    // after the planner's one reply, it's all build
    if (phase !== "explore")
      return route(executor, "build");
    if (editedThisTurn(messages))
      return route(executor, "build");
    // the executor asked for a plan
    return planRequested(messages)
      ? route(planner, "plan")
      : route(executor, "explore");
}

In pi, a "continuation" is any request in the agent loop that isn't a fresh message from you, like the request after a tool result.

Asking for a plan is a tool call

How does Flash say "I've read enough, give me a plan"? It calls a tool named fusion_plan.

The tool takes one argument, a summary of what Flash found and what the task needs. It only exists while Fusion is selected. Its result is the planner's brief:

You are now the planning model. Write a concrete
step-by-step plan (files, exact changes, tests to add
and run) and record it with the todo tool, one item
per step. Do not edit files or run commands. Another
model will carry out the plan.

The router sees that fusion_plan result in the transcript and sends the next request to Pro. Pro sees the whole conversation, including the files Flash already read. Then it writes the plan with the todo tool. You can see that list any time with /todos.

Guardrails, because prompts alone didn't work

Fusion's instructions tell Flash to explore first and call fusion_plan before any edit. A comment in the code explains why that wasn't enough. In a live run, DeepSeek ignored the instruction and edited files directly.

So Fusion now blocks edits in code. While Fusion is selected, the CLI checks every edit and write call:

  • Before a successful fusion_plan call since your last message, the edit is blocked. The model gets back "call fusion_plan first".
  • If the planner tries to edit, it's blocked too. The planner records the plan, and the executor makes the changes.

A few more cases are handled:

  • The planner stops early. If Pro replies with text and no tool calls, the turn would end with nothing built. Fusion adds one hidden message, "The plan is recorded. Carry out the unfinished todo items now", so Flash picks up the work. This happens at most once per plan.
  • The planner request fails. The retry goes to Flash in build mode instead of trying Pro again.
  • A model is missing. If either model can't be found, every request goes to the default model instead of failing.

What stays with Flash

Plain questions skip the planner. Fusion's instructions tell Flash to answer a message that needs no file changes directly, with no fusion_plan call.

Background work also goes to Flash. A compaction summary, for example, is a request outside the agent loop, and the router always sends those to the executor.

The server picks the pair

The model ids aren't hardcoded forever. On startup the CLI calls /client-version, and the server can send a fusion field with a planner and an executor. Today it says:

{
  "planner": "deepseek-v4-pro",
  "executor": "deepseek-v4-flash"
}

The CLI uses that pair only if both models are in the catalog it just loaded. Otherwise it falls back to its built-in pair. So I can swap the planner on the server without shipping a new CLI.

When to use it

Fusion fits tasks where a bad plan costs you more than a slow start:

  • Changes that touch several files.
  • A feature plus the tests for it.
  • Refactors where the order of steps matters.

For a one-line fix, plain DeepSeek V4 Flash is usually the better pick. Under Fusion, even a tiny edit waits for exploration and a planning request.

Trade-offs

  • The plan request costs more. Pro is the more expensive model, so its request uses more of your daily allowance than a Flash request. The /model picker shows how fast each model uses it.
  • Prompt caches don't carry over. pi's docs say switching models loses the prompt cache. Each switch between Flash and Pro sends the context without it.
  • Shell commands aren't blocked. Exploration needs bash, so Fusion leaves it alone. A shell command can still change files before the plan exists. Keep your work in git.
  • One plan per message. Pro writes the plan once. If the build goes sideways, send a new message and Fusion starts over from explore.

Wrapping up

Fusion is a small router on top of pi. Flash explores, Pro writes one plan into the todo list, and Flash builds it. Edits stay blocked until the plan exists, and failures fall back to Flash instead of stalling. Use it for multi-file work, and stay on Flash for quick fixes.

Try it free with npx free-pi-cli@latest, pick Fusion in /model, and read more at www.freepi.ai.

title: 11 tools in my MCP server, 3 of them did 91% of the calls: what I ask before adding a 12th
description:
Two weeks ago the MCP server behind my orchestrator exposed 11 tools. It exposes 4 now. Nothing the agent does changed, because three of those 11 were already doing 91% of the work and I had never bothered to count.

The orchestrator is a small thing I run for content operations: it plans slots, drafts copy, schedules what passes review. Every step talks to the same MCP server, which I maintain, which means every bad decision in it is mine. I went looking because of the token bill. I stayed because of the errors.

What the log said

I turned on one structured line per tool call and left it for 16 days. 427 runs, 1,318 calls.

jq -r 'select(.event=="tool_call") | .tool' calls.ndjson \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

    612 get_content_brief
    402 save_draft
    187 list_pending_slots
     54 get_brand_voice
     33 publish_draft
     18 schedule_post
      7 get_channel_stats
      3 search_published
      2 update_slot_status

Nine lines for eleven tools. archive_draft and get_competitor_feed never showed up at all, which is the kind of absence uniq -c will never tell you about. The top three add up to 1,201 of 1,318 calls, a bit over 91%.

All eleven definitions ride along in every request. I ran the tool block through the tokenizer the model actually uses and got a bit over 6,400 tokens. The three tools doing the work account for about 1,900 of those. So on each of those 1,318 calls I paid to re-send roughly 4,500 tokens of JSON schema describing tools the model mostly ignored. Somewhere near 5.9 million tokens of context spent on a menu.

Then the failures. 37 calls came back with argument validation errors, and 29 of them were the model reaching for publish_draft when it meant schedule_post, or the reverse. I put the two descriptions side by side and I would have gotten it wrong too.

[
  { "name": "publish_draft",  "description": "Publish a draft to its channel." },
  { "name": "schedule_post",  "description": "Publish a draft to its channel at a given time." }
]

The second one is the first one with an extra argument. Blaming the model for that is cheap.

I am not the only person running this math this month. A post here about cutting an MCP server from 15 tools to 4 pulled 76 comments against 61 reactions, a ratio you almost never see on this site, and more argument than applause usually means nobody agrees on where the line goes. InfoQ reported this week that Uber put a gateway in front of more than 800 MCP servers and over 5,000 tools, with incremental discovery so an agent never sees the whole catalogue at once. Same problem, four orders of magnitude up.

The fix I tried first and threw away

My first move was the clever one: collapse everything into a single call tool with an action string and a free-form payload, dispatched server side. The tool block dropped to a little over 300 tokens and I was briefly very pleased with myself.

Then the agent started inventing actions. create_brief. draft_save. Names that read exactly like my own convention and did not exist. Across 90 runs, something like 1 in 6 calls needed a retry, because an enum the model cannot see is an enum the model will guess. The schema was not overhead, it was the contract. I put it back and went after the list instead.

The three questions

Does it write? Then what undoes it?

Every write tool in the registry has to name the tool that reverses it, as a required field. If I cannot name the inverse, the agent does not get the tool. That killed archive_draft in about four seconds: the unarchive was me running an UPDATE by hand, which is not an undo the agent can reach.

type ToolSpec = {
  name: string;
  mode: "read" | "write";
  undo?: string;      // required when mode === "write"
  owner: string;      // a person, not a team alias
  secret?: string;    // credential id this tool uses
  rotatedAt?: string;
};

for (const t of tools) {
  if (t.mode === "write" && !t.undo) {
    throw new Error(`write tool ${t.name} has no documented undo`);
  }
  if (t.mode === "write" && !t.owner) {
    throw new Error(`write tool ${t.name} has no owner`);
  }
}

It fails at boot, not at runtime. The secret and rotatedAt fields are there for the question nobody asks until something leaks: each tool is a credential with a blast radius, and an agent that holds nine of them holds nine keys. Mine had two tools sharing one API key whose last rotation I could not date.

Reading only the descriptions, would I pick the right one?

Hide the names, read the one-liners, choose. If two tools differ only by an argument, they are one tool. publish_draft and schedule_post became one publish_draft with an optional at. Over the following 16 days, wrong-tool errors went from 37 to 3, and two of those three were my planner sending a bad payload.

This is the question that pays fastest, and it costs nothing but reading your own manifest as a stranger would.

Does it earn its schema?

Calls per week against tokens of definition, every request, forever. get_channel_stats: 7 calls in 16 days, around 480 tokens riding along 1,318 times. It did not earn it.

None of the deleted tools disappeared. They moved behind a second call. list_capabilities returns names and one-line summaries, and the full schema for a group arrives only when the agent asks for it. The planning step sees 4 tools. The rare paths pay their own cost at the moment they are used, which is the same trick Uber's gateway does with a much bigger catalogue.

Where it landed

Four tools in the default surface: get_content_brief, save_draft, list_pending_slots, publish_draft. Tool block down from a bit over 6,400 tokens to about 2,050. Wrong-tool errors from 37 to 3 over a comparable window. The agent has asked for the discovery group 9 times in 16 days, and get_competitor_feed is still at zero, so it will probably come out of the registry entirely.

One number I will not claim: latency. The p50 of the planning step went from around 9s to under 7s, but I changed the tool list and the prompt in the same week, so attributing that to the schema would be a story, not a measurement.

And one thing I genuinely do not know how to scale. The undo rule works because the registry has one maintainer. With nine teams publishing tools into a shared gateway, somebody is going to type undo: "manual" and move on, and the boot assertion will pass while the guarantee quietly stops existing.

So: hard cap on the default surface, or discovery from day one? And what do you do with a write tool whose only inverse is a human with database access?

Originally published on the Revin blog.

title: Valid JSON, Wrong Order: Five Structured-Output Myths and a Three-Gate Replay Test
description:
A pipeline of mine broke last week. Not on a timeout. Not on a 500.

It broke because the model returned 'quantity': '3'. A string. Twelve downstream orders went out with a quantity of zero.

So let me ask the boring question. Would your tests have caught that? Mine did not, and I wrote them.

Here are five claims I keep hearing about structured output. Each one comes with evidence you can collect yourself, and a corrected mental model.

Myth 1: JSON mode means my schema is enforced

No. It means the bytes parse as JSON. That is a syntax promise, not a contract.

I keep seeing this confusion in reviews. Someone enables a JSON flag and deletes the validator. Type drift then walks straight into the database.

Evidence you can collect in ten minutes: save 50 raw responses, then run them through json.loads. Count the parses. Then run the parses through a real schema validator. The two numbers will differ.

Corrected model: JSON mode protects the parser. Your schema protects the domain.

Myth 2: If it parses, the model was right
